paragraphs.text: In the divine words of Paul, the great herald, it is good and just, and welcome to all who choose to live piously, to share in the commemorations of the saints. As that song of David says, "The memory of the righteous is accompanied by praises," and, "Praise befits the upright." It is also fitting and desirable for everyone to keep their valiant contests and achievements always in memory by seeing them in images. In the same way it is holy and pious that their deeds be told in written books. Both of these, coming to us through sight and through hearing, lead us toward the virtue of the originals and the godly [?] [variant reading: "of the righteous." The title is:] The Life, Conduct and Contest, with a Partial Account of the Miracles, of the Holy [?]

[?] zeal. In them is fulfilled that saying of sacred Scripture: "Show me your face, and let me hear your voice." For both are seen through an image and sent to the ear through the written word. Seeing an image comes from those who skilfully possess that art. But the word that is heard comes from those who have been initiated into divine things by the divine Spirit and by learning and knowledge. I myself have no share in either of these. So I am overcome by fear, and I lack the courage for this undertaking, to open my mouth and stretch out my hand, in case speaking brings on me the grievous fate of the rash. For, as the proverb says and as it is written, "A man's own lips are a strong snare," and each person is caught by the words of his own mouth, and "the reward of his lips will be given to him." For great and beloved is the holy martyr Stephen, who leads this spiritual festival, and the nothingness of my poor mind is very small. Where shall I find a crown of praises for his life to offer him? I am quite at a loss, beloved, as to how I can describe the brilliance and toil of his way of life, or how I can tell of the daring of his prize-winning martyrdom. For the wonders he performed by grace from above are marvellous to tell. They shake my reasoning and amaze it, and force it beyond its proper bounds. Still, I will not hesitate to speak as far as my mind allows. Failing to praise him as he deserves is no cause for condemnation, but failing to speak as far as one's ability reaches deserves blame. So, measuring my thought to my speech, I, who have never attempted anything of this kind, have been urged on and have given myself to the task with all my strength. I have kept in mind the condemned disobedience of our ancestress Eve, and I have thought about the wicked servant who buried his talent in the ground. I also feared that with the passing of time such a life of our venerable Father might be forgotten. For just as a cloud can hide the sun, so time can cover over what is not spoken of. Forty-two years have now passed since our all-blessed Father Stephen underwent his holy end through martyrdom. Urged on, I have gathered this life from truthful men and from his disciples. I ran about here and there, collecting what concerned him from his tender infancy to old age, the delightful and wonderful accounts of his birth and of his death. I gathered them as if from the depths of a long time and recovered them from oblivion. In this I imitated the industrious bee, which gathers from many flowers what is useful for making honey. But let Christ our true God lead the way, "who enlightens every man coming into the world,"

[?] the only mind of those who think, and of what is piously thought; the word of those who speak and of what is spoken; who is and becomes all things to all; who gives the light of instruction so that we know when we ought to speak a word. For "the revelation of his words will give light and understanding to the simple." So much for this. But I do not want to stretch out the discourse with longer digressions. Keeping to the course set before me, I now come to introduce the beginning of this life that was pleasing to God. Only, you too must strive alongside me with your prayers. Make God gracious toward my worthless life, and ask that a word be given me when I open my mouth. Then I will not be judged as one who laid hold of things beyond his worth and brought nothing precious worthy of the subject, which would not suit even my weakness, provided no kind of carelessness is joined to it [?]. Besides this I rely on the grace from above, which gives each person what suits them, and from which "every good gift and every perfect present comes from above," descending on those who are worthy of the Spirit. So, as I said, I will come to the very beginning of his life. I have found an excellent and swift ally in the help of prayers on both sides. And you, sacred assembly of the Orthodox, all of you who have tasted, even with the tip of a finger, the philosophy that is according to Christ: take care to lend the ears of your mind with fervour and in true faith. For in what follows the story is about spiritual health, not about fleshly glory or advancement, as it is among the pagans. This man, then, is the rich and joyful host of this sacred banquet and of all of you who have come as guests to listen. He shares both the name and the character of the protomartyr, in name and in deed. He is no stranger to the Byzantines, nor a foreigner to those who live in the imperial city. For he is one of us: born, raised and sacrificed here, known to our fathers, a whole burnt offering they saw with their own eyes. In the time of Artemius, also called Anastasius Augustus, in the first year of his reign and in the year 6222 from the creation of the world, there was a well-known man in Constantinople. He was not one of those distinguished by rank, nor one of those conspicuous for wealth gained through impiety. He belonged to those who live in self-sufficiency, to use the Apostle's words, and he supported himself by the work of his own hands, from which he also shared with the needy as far as he could. This man lived on the slope of the imperial public avenue, where the Stavrion stands and gives the place its name. Below it, on the downward side, there are large houses called Ta Konsta. The God-loving man lived in these houses with a wife of like character, both of them raised in piety, and two daugh-

ters were born to them, one after the other, some time apart. When they had been born and had reached a suitable age, the honourable pair of parents brought up their well-born pair of daughters in letters and in a piety like their own. But their most pious mother saw that time was flowing on and that her womanly condition was nearing barrenness. She was distressed and grieved, because she had no male child. Carried along by unhesitating faith, she called to mind Sarah, Hannah and Elizabeth, and thought of that saying of Scripture: "He who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened." So she imitated her namesake Hannah, for Anna was her name too. Just as Hannah did in the tabernacle of the Law, she never stopped visiting the venerable churches of the all-immaculate Mother of God. Above all she went every day to her most venerable church at Blachernae, and she never missed the all-night vigil of praise held on Friday evening. There she offered prayers of supplication, standing opposite the holy image of the Mother of God, in which she was depicted holding her Son and God in her arms. Weeping before the common helper and salvation of our race, she said: "O shelter of those who run to you, Theotokos, anchor and protectress of those who seek you in their grief; most saving harbour of those sinking from despondency in the sea of life, and most ready helper of those who call on you for aid in their despair; glory of mothers and adornment of daughters; by your divine and human childbearing you changed the shameful condemnation that our foremother Eve brought on all womankind into joyful confidence. Have mercy on me and hear me. Break the bond within me, as you broke that of your mother Anna when she gave birth to you. By your motherly intercession grant that I bear a male child, so that I may offer him as a gift to your Son and God." The woman said this two and three times. Then, during one of her prayers, after making her customary genuflection, she fell asleep. And she who is swiftest to help our race, bending her Son to mercy as a mother, changed the despondent woman's sorrow into a mother's joy in the following way. In that very hour she appeared to the woman as in a vision, looking just like the icon described above. She struck [?] her on the hip and raised her up, saying: "Go away rejoicing [?], woman, for you have a son." The woman got up, alarmed within herself, and found the vigil of praise at its end. She returned home singing hymns, and she conceived in her womb. At the time of that conception, Germanus, our common Father, the orthodox teacher of the Church's doctrines, was entrusted by God's decree with the helm of the [?] city. He was brought up from Cyzicus like an all-resplendent lamp. He was not put under the bushel but was placed on the lampstand that had borne him, so that he might shine, as [?]

upon the whole world. At his enthronement the whole world under the sun came running together: people of every age, old and elderly, young men and youths, adolescents, and newborn babies still sucking at the breast all came together. If I may say so, even angels came down to that joyful installation. Together with all of them came also these two fruitful shoots of a pious union. They saw the vast crowd of people, and the honourable Anna wanted to turn back because of the crush of the crowd, with everyone pressing and jostling one another. She feared that under such pressure she might lose the unborn child before its time and that it would die. But her most honourable husband would not agree. Being very manly and stronger in body than others, he told her to hold on to his sides with her hands. He went in front, pushing forward and being pushed back, and at last they barely managed to burst into the forecourts of the great sanctuary of the Wisdom of God. From there they made their way freely into the portico in front of the church's gates. There they climbed onto a bench and waited for the entrance of Germanus, the sacred initiator. For truly many praises had been spoken of him, and everyone was drawn there just to see him with their own eyes. Then, as that high priest was making his entrance, she was moved by God and saw him as a flame of fire, as she affirmed with oaths to those who told me. At once she cried out: "All-holy one, bless my son in my womb!" The luminary gently turned his eye and looked at the woman. Moved by the fire of the divine Spirit, the initiator into the mysteries said: "Woman, may the Lord bless the fruit of your womb according to your faith, through the intercessions of the Theotokos and of the protomartyr Stephen." Truly, good faith receives an even better reward! The Canaanite woman once heard from Christ the Saviour, "Woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish." In the same way this woman received her answer from the divine Father who bore the whole of Christ within himself, and she received even more: the name of the child who was to be born. When the usual liturgy had been completed, all had received the divine and immaculate mysteries of Christ, and everyone had gone home after the dismissal in peace. Some days later, when her time was fulfilled, this truly most God-loving new Anna gave birth to a new Samuel in the spirit. As soon as he was born, they named him Stephen, after the protomartyr, according to the prediction of our venerable father Germanus. When the eighth day had passed and the infant was brought to the church of God, he received the name that had been decided beforehand. Likewise on the fortieth day his mother, carrying him in her own

arms, as the celebrated Hannah carried Samuel, who was holy from infancy, came with her husband to the venerable church of the Theotokos at Blachernae. There she had made her prayer and received what she asked for. Standing again before that divine icon, she gave thanks with tears of joy and said: "Hail, all-pure one, who ended my barrenness so that I could bear a male child. Hail, all-immaculate one, who turned my despondency into joy. Hail, swiftest salvation of those who seek you. For I, wretched woman, sought you and found you, and I received more than I asked: not only a child, but also his name, from your servant who is now our shepherd." Stretching her hands upward, and reverently laying the infant at the feet of that holy icon, she cried out again: "Receive, O Lady, the offspring of your motherly intercession. Receive, my guarantor, the child who was promised to you before his conception. Receive, lender, the loan from your debtors." Her God-loving husband was struck speechless at the length of her prayer and the flood of her tears, and he stood there astounded. She took him by the hand, pointed to the divine likeness, and said: "She, my sweetest husband, is the guarantor, protectress and helper of Stephen's birth." Both bowed their heads and venerated that holy ground, giving thanks to the guarantor and protectress of all Christians, and then they went home. Truly, through her thanksgiving the noble mother prophetically pointed to the one who would later bear witness for the icon of Christ and of his Mother, as will become clear further on. When the holy and life-giving Resurrection of the Saviour came, the parents took up the child, who was holy from infancy, and came to the baptistery of the most holy Great Church of God on the evening of Holy Saturday. They presented the holy youth for the washing of regeneration, and he was baptized in the name of the life-giving Trinity by the all-blessed luminary Germanus himself. After the anointing with the divine chrism, his mother fell at the feet of the God-bearing chief shepherd and cried: "Honoured Father, pray for the one whose name you made known while he was still in the womb." The honourable Germanus would not agree to say another prayer beyond the anointing with chrism. But he took hold of the father's head with one hand, pointed to the infant with the other, and said: "May God, who enlightens every man coming into the world, make this child like the one whose name he has received." And so they went home with a blessing. Such were the beginnings of our God-bearing Father Stephen. These are the delightful and true accounts of his conception, birth,

naming and illumination. Now let the account of his later God-given achievements begin. For if the forecourts are like this, the inner rooms must be far finer. The honoured font, mother of us all, gave new birth to this holy man in a spiritual childbirth. She gave him mystical milk to drink as if from a breast. Then she set before him, as solid food, the knowledge of divine ideas, which those whose senses are trained to tell good from evil are appointed to eat. As we said, she raised him like a mother and nourished him, and trained him to keep vigil over divine studies. She made his life radiant, adorned his soul and led it up to the heights. She made him a friend of God and prepared him to look down on the things of this world. In short, she received him when he came into this world out of non-being, and she welcomed him again when he departed from here. She waits to become a witness of his excellence when the Judge gives everyone the reward they deserve. But without noticing, I have strayed into these words and left behind what should have been said first. I am no better than those who try to build the roof of a house before its foundations. So from here I steer the course of my discourse forward again. The parents of this most holy child saw that he had passed the age of infancy and reached his sixth year, and that he ought now to be busy with lessons. So they handed him over to be taught the first elements of sacred letters. He delighted in his lessons every day without ceasing and surpassed everyone, attending not only to his studies but also to every virtue. He never failed to go out at night with his holy mother to the customary vigils held on the commemorations of the saints. This honourable youth received such grace that when the reading was done during the kathismata, he would stand before the holy screen and pay attention to the reader. Simply by listening he learned what was read and knew it by heart, whether it was the account of a martyrdom, a saint's life, or the teaching of some Father. He followed the common teacher and was sober in all things, "forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead" day by day. To speak in David's words, he never stopped meditating on the law of the Lord day and night, "like a tree planted by streams of water." For he knew

that before long, in his own season, he would yield the fruits of his labours a hundredfold. So the honourable Stephen was trained in the highest piety, and in a short time he surpassed many of his own age in his soul's love of God and love of learning. His eagerness was beyond his years, so that his parents marvelled at him and said, "Truly this is a son of prayer." In these things, then, the holy youth was trained and shaped. His formation was the best and purest kind. As the clear-voiced and most theological mind says, the divine David rightly calls this formation "of the day," the opposite of that "of the night." As he learned the divine Scriptures, he longed to imitate the divine men who appear in them. Following their example, he gave no thought at all to varied foods, did not seek vainglory, and never stopped his mouth from giving glory to God. During the years of his schooling, Leo, the Syrian by birth, the new Doeg and Edomite, came from the regions of the East and rose up against the emperor Theodosius in a rebellious conspiracy. Theodosius judged it wrong for Christians to fight Christians. He took up a life of quiet retirement and left the impious man to enjoy what he desired and the imperial rank. At once the tyrant went into the palace, the dog to the holy things, the swine to the pearls. He took on the colour of a fox and spent his first years in deceit. Out of respect for the great president Germanus, he counted himself among the pious. But after the tenth year of his rule, this new Belshazzar breathed into the Church a Manichaean heresy, perhaps even, if I may say so, a rival of the Aphthartodocetae. He assembled the people under his rule, and in the midst of them all the savage beast, who bore the name of a lion, roared like a lion. From his wrathful heart, as from Mount Etna, he belched out fire and brimstone in that pitiful utterance. He said: "Since making images is a craft of idolatry, we must not venerate them." At this utterance the Christ-loving and orthodox people were troubled and groaned. The wretch immediately kept silent about the rest and turned his speech to a different opinion. Truly, "his throat is an open grave," and his heart is a whitewashed wall. When Germanus, the herald of piety, learned of this, he stood up against the tyrant's rebellious opinion and declared to him: "Emperor, our Master Christ, our Saviour and God, became flesh from the immaculate blood of the holy Theotokos and appeared as a perfect man like us and able to be depicted. Since then all idolatrous worship has vanished, and every idol has been consigned to fire and darkness. From the time he lived among us, and from the world-saving teaching of his apostles, until now, seven hundred and thirty-six years have passed; and those throughout

…the righteous Fathers who have lived through the times in between never conceived any such thing about the holy and venerable icons. From the very beginning, after Christ's ascension into heaven, the image was given visible form. The woman with the flow of blood set up a statue of the Saviour to mark the miracle done for her. Besides this there is the image not made by hands in the city of Edessa, and also the icon of the all-pure Theotokos painted by Luke the evangelist and sent from Jerusalem to Theophilus. The holy ecumenical councils, too, found these icons already in use and decreed that they should be venerated and not rejected. Know this well, O emperor: if you hold to this course, I will readily die for the holy and venerable icons. The icon of Christ bears his holy name, the name by which he appeared in the flesh and lived among men. It is right and holy to die for his name in every way. Whoever dishonours his icon directs the insult at the one portrayed in it." When the lawless emperor heard this, he roared like the lion whose name he bore. He sent sword-bearing officials to the patriarchal residence and ordered them to drive the saint out of it with blows and insults. When he had gone down and taken up the monastic life, the whole city could be seen pouring out lamentation and loud wailing, because it had been robbed of the Father's honey-sweet teaching. That day was not a day but darkness, lamentation and woe upon woe, as the prophet says. In these ill-omened days the impious Anastasius laid hold of the high priesthood with the hand of impiety, by military force and not by the vote of God and of piety. He handed over all the affairs of the Church to the palace. Having seized power in this way, the tyrant of the heresy at once tried to take down the holy icon of Christ our God and Master that stood above the imperial gates, at the place called the holy Chalke because of its appearance, and to commit it to the fire. And he did so. But while it was being taken down, some honourable women were strengthened by divine zeal. They rushed in boldly, seized the ladder, threw the spatharios who was removing the icon to the ground, dragged him about and put him to death. Then they ran straight to the patriarchal residence, stoned the impious Anastasius and said: "Most foul head and enemy of the truth, is this why you seized the priesthood, to destroy the holy and sacred offerings?" The unholy man could not bear this defeat and fled from the presence of the pious women. He took refuge with the tyrant and persuaded him to have those holy women put to death by the sword. And so it was done. Having contended for the icon of Christ, they received the prize from Christ, and they rejoice in the kingdom of heaven together with all the holy prize-winning martyrs. [Variant reading: "betrayed" [?].]

So for a long time in that period Constantinople remained in this darkness and clung to the heresy. Those living in it piously and in orthodoxy were deeply disheartened, and many of them left their homeland and moved to orthodox towns. The parents of the blessed Stephen were caught up in these troubles too and looked about for their own salvation. But they were held back because they wished to fulfil the pledge they had made for their child. They reflected that it was [not?] possible to keep him for long in the monasteries of Byzantium because of the turmoil the tyrant had stirred up. Moved by God and guided by an angel, they acted as Joseph, the father of God, once did when he fled into Egypt with the Theotokos from the face of Herod the slayer of infants. They too left their homeland with their godly son Stephen and sailed across to the harbour of Chalcedon. From there they took the road leading to the mountain of our holy and God-bearing Father Auxentius. On this mountain our great and wonder-working Father Auxentius had lived in earlier times. From there he sent out the rays of his miracles into the whole world and made the faith clear, contending bravely against the impious Dioscorus and Eutyches at the holy fourth ecumenical council, which met at Chalcedon. This mountain stands opposite those sailing into the gulf of Nicomedia, in the province of Bithynia. It is most delightful for those who wish to be saved. It is higher than all the hills around it, cold and dry, and to put it briefly, it touches heaven. One could call it the mountain of God and Mount Horeb, Mount Carmel or Mount Sinai, Tabor or Lebanon, or a holy city, since it lies on a mountain like the one in Jerusalem, and one would not miss the fitting name. For wherever there is a place of salvation that draws one's way of life toward being saved, there is truly the real Jerusalem. On this holy mountain, then, which has carried the name of Saint Auxentius from his day until now and will carry it for ever, the Fathers who held the mountain in succession shut themselves up in the holy cave and found paradise in exchange for death. After the death of our divine Father Auxentius, his disciple Sergius lived in the cave. After him the third was Bendemianus, a worker of wonders who shone in every way in the virtues [?]. Then the fourth was Gregory, a man of self-control, crowned with holy grey hair. After him the fifth was the venerable John, a new Abraham, who shared in the gift of foresight. It was to this holy John that the godly pair Gregory and Anna brought their honoured son Stephen at that time, like an offering. They entreated him to receive the boy and to count him worthy of the holy and angelic habit, [?] of prayer. [Note: "opposite" is missing in one manuscript. Variant reading: "lying". One manuscript has "place" instead of "way of life".]

They said that he was their son and that even before his birth, from the womb, he had been dedicated to the monastic rank. As has been said, that venerable old man was full of the gift of foresight. He perceived the youth's great simplicity, his gait, the cheerfulness of his face, his knit brows, and in short all the divine grace that was in him. He said: "May God bless you, child, and make you a chosen vessel." And he said quietly to his parents: "Truly the Spirit of God has come to rest on this boy." The customary service was held, and when the time for the morning vigil and doxology came, after the usual completion of the canon, our God-bearing Father John took him in front of the holy cave, since John himself never went out. He instructed him at length and said: "Blessed are you, Stephen my child, because today you receive the second font, putting on light upon light, and the second baptism guards the first. Blessed are you, child, because today you fulfil the voice of Christ as the Gospel says: you leave father and mother and sisters and everything that is here today and gone tomorrow, and you carry his cross on your shoulders so that you may inherit the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you, child, because like the prophet you have chosen to be cast aside in the house of God rather than live in the tents and the city of heretics who accuse Christians. Consider, child, the calling of the monastic dignity: our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, as Paul, the chosen vessel, says. Consider, child, whom you are enlisting with. Do not again let longing for your parents come before God. For he both formed you and saved you, while parents have destroyed those they loved and handed them over to punishment, as the author of the enlightening Ladder says. Take care, child, not to turn back. For this too is written: no one who puts his hand to the plough and turns back is fit for the kingdom of heaven." He taught him these things and much more. Then he asked for the scissors, received them from Stephen's hands, and tonsured him in the sixteenth year of his age. He clothed him in the angelic habit. When the customary rites that follow had been completed, the saint's parents left the mountain and returned home, praising and glorifying God. The venerable Stephen stripped for the contests and attended to the provisions that lead to virtue. He gave God the fruit proper to each season. When he suspected gluttony, his fruit was self-control. When thoughts of some bodily pleasure came upon him, chastity sprang up in him again. He mastered anger and wrath so thoroughly [Variant readings: "most gifted"; "steady character". Variant readings: "consequently"; "following".]

that one could say of him in the prophet's words: "Like a deaf man who does not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth." He bore the fruit of love and patience. In this way he overcame everything and conquered the storms of imagination that thoughts stir up. The God-bearing John was amazed at his virtue in all things and said: "Child, hold back from so much fasting because of the bitter cold of the mountain and the violent blast of the winds. Otherwise you may grow too weak to do your service." For Stephen served the saint in his needs and brought water from a long way off. He fetched it from the southern part of the mountain, on its gently sloping side. There lies the cemetery of our holy Father Auxentius, which he built while he was still alive and living on the mountain. He also founded a monastery of holy women there and named it Trichinareai, either because the place is rough and hard to reach, or because of the thorny, hard and very rough clothing of hair that the nuns wore. That holy house is preserved to this day and shines with its way of life, through the prayers of the holy Fathers. From this hard-to-reach place, as has been said, the all-blessed Stephen carried water and everything else needed, in burning heat and in winter, and he never flagged or abandoned his usual rule. Instead he made a new beginning every day, eager and untouched by passions and demons. He followed in the footsteps of his revered master John and never stopped learning from him how to care for salvation. This wise John was such a man that he could call even four-footed animals by name with a human voice, and they brought him what he needed and carried back answers. Let no one think what I am about to say incredible. You know, holy brothers, that if someone keeps the image and likeness, not only wild animals but even the elements themselves submit to him. The witnesses of this are the three youths in the fire; Moses, Joshua, Elijah and Elisha in the water; and Daniel and Jonah among the beasts. But why cite many examples? In the same way this divine Father John kept a little dog on the mountain. At that time there were many monasteries in those mountains, which the impious new Babylonian razed like a tyrant because he loved hunting. If it happened that the holy Stephen was not on the hill but away on some errand, and some monks from the surrounding mountains came to visit John, this godly Father would call the dog by name and write a note saying what he needed for the visiting brothers. He would tie the note [Variant readings: "mastered"; "be reckoned"; "present".]

to the dog's neck and say to it within the visitors' hearing: "Go down to the monastery, take this note to the abbess, and come back quickly." At once the dog went to the monastery as the Father had commanded, barked at the abbess's cell and so carried out its orders. The nuns [?] of the monastery knew the animal's service, so they immediately brought it in to the abbess and did what the note said. When this was done the dog went back up the mountain to its holy masters. Another time the most venerable Stephen came back up the mountain from some errand and found the God-bearing John with his holy head laid against the little window of the cave, weeping bitterly. Stephen went in and made the customary prostration, but he received no response, because the Father was in deep distress. Lying on the ground, he wondered what the Father's weeping could mean. That gentle Father knew the saint's thoughts by God's revelation. He raised him up and said: "My lament is for you, my most honoured child. I know that in your time this place will grow and then be overthrown by the heresy of the icon-burners that is now boiling up." The venerable Stephen groaned painfully from his heart and said: "O Father, will I perish with them in their impiety and not be saved?" The holy John said: "No, child. But take heed, for it is written: whoever endures to the end will be saved." And he foretold to him everything that was going to happen to him. At that time the venerable Stephen's father came to the end of his life. So Stephen went to the city and attended his father's funeral. After the burial he sold everything they owned in Constantinople. Then he left the homeland with his mother and one of his sisters, since the other had already been tonsured in another monastery in Byzantium, and they came to the mountain. The venerable Stephen had his mother and sister blessed by the holy old man John and instructed in the word of truth. Then he brought them down to the women's monastery and enrolled them in that holy community. Through the holy habit he became the spiritual father of his mother in the flesh, and of his sister as well. When the rite of the holy habit had been completed, he went back up the mountain and resumed his former way of life. The God-bearing John, having excelled in all works pleasing to God, fell asleep in peace and

departed well from this world. He had instructed Saint Stephen in a great many things, and his last words were: "Farewell, child. But be on your guard for the outcome of the danger that is coming upon you." The godly Stephen was not downcast at this but rather cheerful. He struck the semantron and so made the Father's falling-asleep known. Then a choir of ascetics could be seen running together from the surrounding mountains, hills, slopes and glens, like deer driven by thirst, to the mountain of the spring of the God-bearing Auxentius, to embrace the God-bearing John for the last time and bury him. So his venerable and holy body was laid in the cemetery of the Fathers, and his honoured soul was carried by God's angels up to heaven, rejoicing for ever. It is fitting to pass from glory to glory and from saint to saint, for the number of God's servants is never lacking. When Moses died, Joshua son of Nun was there. When Elijah was taken up, Elisha was at once recognized as the heir of his mantle and of a double share of his grace. In the same way, when the God-bearing John departed this world, the venerable Stephen was recognized as the heir of his way of life and of his grace in double measure, and much more. For he had received the first share of John's teachings, and so he had to come close to equalling the blessed man's God-loving works, and this he showed. As a son takes after his own father, so he reproduced in himself the marks of his own teacher's virtue. This man, then, the founder of the heavenly metropolis and the perfect number among monks, became in due succession the sixth inhabitant of the divine [?] and soul-saving cave. He was a new Jared, who was sixth from Adam and was known as the father of Enoch for a like pleasing of God. Stephen too is known as the sixth from the all-blessed Auxentius. As the prophet says, he conceived the fear of God as a son, and through martyrdom he brought forth the pleasing of God, like a new Enoch, the first of those who pleased God. He grieved at his master's departure, was distressed and troubled, and resolved above all, as a good follower, to carry on his teacher's contest. Think of those who are used to crossing the broad back of the sea and making long voyages. The nature of water has no marked roads, and its thin, yielding substance takes no footprints or wheel tracks, so they watch the position of the stars and travel the course before them. From the paths above they clearly work out the track below and make their trackless journey without going astray. Or think of those who embrace life in the desert [?]. When they want to visit one another they do not trust themselves

to paths they do not know, because they fear losing their way and dread the ambushes of robbers. Instead they keep to the highways and complete their journey in great safety. In the same way our all-blessed Father Stephen wished to cross the sea of a hard life and was eager to travel to the Jerusalem above. Like stars guiding his steps from on high, he kept before his eyes the interpreters of the life pleasing to God, the five holy Fathers who had lived in the holy cave in succession, from Auxentius to John. In his mind he followed their dwelling, worn smooth by them like a royal highway, and was eager to walk in it. So he went to the narrow little cell and shut himself up in the underground rock in the thirty-first year of his age. He took up the sixth lot after the fifth, completing, as one might say, the number of a six-starred radiance. Trained in the love of stillness to the highest degree, he stayed there and owned absolutely nothing of this age. Like a bee in a hive, this wonderful Stephen shut himself up in the cave of the mountain and diligently made the sweet, unploughed honey of virtue, offering it to God, the King of all. He trained his senses fearlessly until it became habit and he could tell good from worse. He also learned to do that apostolic work of sewing and knotting nets in the fisherman's craft, and calligraphy too, so as not to be a burden to anyone but rather to give to those in need from his own labours. He freed himself from every earthly care and had only one concern: how to please God in prayers and fasting. Moreover, he devoted himself to every virtue. Like an excellent farmer he cut out the thorns of the passions by the roots, demolishing reasonings and every height raised up against the knowledge of God. So he fulfilled the prophet's word: "Break up your fallow ground, and do not sow among thorns." As this all-blessed man practised these things pleasing to God, he became known to everyone, for it is true that a city set on a mountain cannot be hidden. And what came of his excellent way of life? Many people, fired with divine zeal for Christ, ran to him. They begged to live with him and implored him to become their guide in the life according to God. He was reluctant, but they persuaded him in the end. For he felt compelled, since he became all things to all and taught each person to look not only to his own interests but also to seek those of his neighbours, so that they might be saved. From then on brothers came to him, up to twelve in number. He obeyed the command of the Gospel, "Whoever comes to me I will never cast out," and welcomed them most gladly. Like a good trainer, he anointed them for the contests of the ascetic life. And [References: [?] 14; 1 Cor. [?]; John 6:37. Variant reading: "after him". [?]]

First he received Marinus, a good man of gentle character; then John; and after him Zacharias, a man, to tell the truth, well schooled in the spiritual road. Among them were also Christopher and Satan's pair that bites in secret (I mean Sergius and Stephen, who were carried off from God into slavery by the tyrant, and of whom I will tell later), and six others, whose names are in the book of life. With these the mountain was settled like a town, and it took on the form and holiness of a wonderful coenobium. Everything needed, so to speak, was provided without fail by God's bounty and the holy man's prayers: a cemetery and other necessary buildings, and the [?] needed in them. A most devout coenobium was established, bearing the name of Saint Auxentius. The saint-hating tyrant, hostile to the saint, later razed the monastery to the ground and gave the hill the name [?] "of Auxentius," by which his fellow initiates call it to this day. When the coenobium had been fittingly set in order, our father Stephen held fast to the anchor of the word. He guided the community from the God-built cave and exhorted them, saying: "Children, take heed to yourselves and to your souls. Cast off the fear or listlessness that comes from the soul-destroying demons, and love God greatly. Love for him is shown not by the value of the material, or by [?] lavish means, but by largeness of disposition and generosity of will, which shows itself [?] even in the small gifts of your ascetic labour. Likewise, put dejection and grief far from you and come to God cheerfully, always keeping in mind that song of the prophet: 'It is good for me to cling to God, to put my hope in the Lord.' For hope, even when it is only dreamed of, nourishes no less than reality. It beguiles utter despair away with expectation, and with its hand it raises up strength that has fallen. Dejection and grief, on the other hand, drive even those who strive to keep a sober mind in misfortune to blasphemous thoughts. Yet the passion has an excuse: it tyrannizes the grieving man and persuades him to say many things against his will, overcome perhaps by the magnitude of his circumstances. Since, then, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, as the Lord says, and the violent seize it, let us take it in the inward way and [?], as the great herald, the divine Paul, says: [?] afflicted, ill-treated, [?], hungry and thirsty, wandering in deserts and mountains, in caves and holes of the earth. Let us piously pass through this brief sojourn of our much-suffering life here below, so that we may inherit that other life and say to the incorruptible Judge: 'See my humiliation and my

toil, and forgive all my sins.'" So our all-blessed father Stephen enlightened those he had begotten as children in the Lord, and every day he kept at it without ceasing, raising them up toward the restoration of salvation. When his disciples had reached twenty in number, the all-blessed man put Marinus, a man upheld by God, in charge of the stewardship and of all the affairs of the monastery. He himself took up a harsher way of life, his heart's desire being to shut himself in more narrowly than in the confines of the cave. The head of the mountain is crowned by an enormous rock and has a hollow like a ravine on its southern side, where the monastery and the God-built cave lie together. This hollow is sheltered and safe from the winter winds of the north and the southwest because, as was said, it is covered by the crowning rock. Our all-blessed father Stephen went round this summit and built on it, beside the cave, a cell that was tiny in length and breadth, in height and depth: about a cubit and a half wide and about two cubits long. On the eastern side he made a small niche for prayer, so low that he could stand only by stooping; it is preserved to this day. All the rest he left open to the sky [?], wishing to be covered by the roof of heaven not made with hands. He made it so cramped and fearsome that those who saw it said it was scarcely a tomb fit to bury this wretched flesh, let alone a dwelling for a monk to rest in. But let no one suppose, as the fault-finding heretics do, that he thought himself above the Fathers before him. For the God-pleasing Life of our forefather Auxentius records that Auxentius had the cage of his ascetic life on this very summit, where he, a new Elisha to the old Elijah, as if on Mount Carmel, pitched the narrower tent of the sheepskin mantle. Stephen likewise wished to equal the God-bearing Auxentius rather than the other Fathers in between, since he was also younger in age than they had been: he was in his forty-second year when he moved to the summit of the mountain. His disciples did not know why the structure had been built. In the dark, around midnight, the father called Marinus, the man upheld by God, alone, and told him his purpose as to a beloved child. Then, leaving the cave together with him, he went into that most fearsome, tomb-like dwelling. At dawn, after the morning hymns, all the brothers made the customary prostration at the entrance of the cave and asked the saint to give his blessing, but the father's most compassionate voice of prayer, which they heard every day [?], did not sound in their attentive ears. They were at a loss,

and after a long while they got up and ran up [?] finding it. As soon as the brothers heard what he said, they fell quiet, begging only that at least the roof of his cell might be covered over. But he said he was content to be sheltered by the roof of the clouds of heaven. So he was scorched in summer and frozen in winter. As for clothing, his body was enclosed crosswise in irons. From the shoulders to the waist ran irons nailed on both sides to a belt of iron [?] that went all round him, and under the armpits another iron girdle encircled him, to which the middles of the irons coming down from the shoulders were nailed. His tunic was of leather and nothing else, with the holy cowl, the cross-bearing analabos, and likewise the sacred epomis of the monastic habit. To lie down on he had only a small mat, after the example of the God-bearing John, who had been his teacher. While this blameless father lived amid these excellences, it was impossible, as was said before, for him to be hidden, since he was a city founded on that great and holy mountain. So he was shown forth to all as a renowned lamp, especially to the orthodox and devout who lived in the imperial city. Many came to him on the mountain for their benefit, and after being suitably edified by the sight of him alone, they went back home praising and glorifying

God. Among them was a woman devout in spirit and of distinguished rank, who had been left a widow by her husband. Every day she heard from everyone about the godly way of life of our venerable father Stephen. Forgetting the timidity of women, she set out on foot, asking her way again and again, and reached the hill of this most holy shepherd and teacher. When she came near the saint's cell, she asked to receive his prayer. When the father had finished the customary prayer, she rose and in tears told the saint everything about herself, her widowhood and her childlessness, and said, "I long to take up the solitary life, and I seek to be saved." The God-loving father instructed her at length with spiritual words, set out for her what leads to salvation, and sent her away, saying, "See, woman, to whom you have given your word. Do not let death overtake you before you pay what you have pledged." That honourable woman engraved the word of the God-bearing father on her soul, like wax taking an impression, and kept it unspoiled. She reached the harbour of Chalcedon and sailed back to her homeland. She sold all her estates and property in Constantinople and gave most of it to the poor, for she feared the death of the soul, as the venerable father had said, and was eager to fulfil her pledge. Finally she left her own town, leaving behind, as the Gospel bids [?], parents, acquaintances, friends, kin and neighbours. Taking up the cross of Christ, she crossed the Propontis from the city and came to the wonderful mountain, bringing gold to the saint for him to distribute as he saw fit. She made the customary prostration before the cell and said, "Bless me, Father." He answered her sternly: "Does not the Saviour cry out plainly in the Gospel, 'Whoever does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple'? Why do you still carry the remnants of the world about with you after leaving the world?" The woman was astonished at the father's gift of insight and at his stern rebuke, and answered him with the modesty proper to women: "It is not because I am held by a perishable desire for it that I offer this gold, honoured Father, but so that it may be well distributed by your holy hands for the sake of my hardened soul." The God-loving father refused and said, "I cannot put out the sparks of other people's sins with my own hands. Through my negligence one of them might smoulder and kindle a huge blaze in my soul, as some have suffered for this very reason. No, those who sow should also be the ones to reap." The woman said, "Then what do you bid me do, Father?" That most compassionate man, because,

as was said, she had at last left her possessions behind, would not allow her to go back to her homeland. Instead he told her to distribute the gold with her own hands, together with Marinus, the man upheld by God, in the villages that lay close by. Having thus stripped her of the swept-up dung of this life, he gave her the holy habit and renamed her Anna, and he became her father and sponsor in the Lord. He then sent her at once to the lower monastery and entrusted her to the holy and devout mother who presided over it, urging that honourable woman earnestly to watch over everything that concerned the salvation of her soul.

The time has now come, and it presses me to make known his athletic contests. Yet, struck by my own conscience, I try to hold my tongue, since I will not be equal to recounting the weight of the undertaking, poor as I am in word and deed. For somehow the glory of deeds is endangered by the words that tell them. Those who choose to attend not to the truth but to the cleverness of words like to judge deeds by the weakness or strength of the telling, as outsiders do with their myths. Nevertheless, I have given rein and yielded to those who urge me, taking courage from this divine holy martyr, and trusting that through the prayers of those who urged me to this he can grant me ample resources. Let that song of David be set before us against the heresy of the innovating accusers of Christians and burners of icons: "Many times they have fought against me from my youth," says the Prophet somewhere, foretelling the continual uprisings that would come against the Church. And, prophesying its invincibility in its contests, he adds: "Let Israel now say: Many times they have fought against me from my youth, and yet they could not prevail against me." This could never fit Israel according to the flesh. The Egyptians enslaved it, foreign peoples often overcame it, the Babylonians enslaved it and led it away captive, the Macedonians devoured it cruelly and bitterly, and at last the Romans gave it over to utter destruction and made it scattered, exiled and sojourning throughout the world. They made its habitation desolate and, as the prophet says, bent its back for ever. But God's newly chosen Israel, which truly sees God and with unveiled face beholds the glory of the Lord as in a mirror — the new Israel, I mean, the flock bought by Christ, prefigured by Jacob, who was renamed Israel and who thrust aside his elder brother as unworthy and took both the birthright and his father's blessing — this Israel might fittingly say: "Many times they have fought against me from my youth, and yet they could not prevail against me." From its earliest age countless phalanxes of enemies rose up against it at once. They attacked but did not conquer; they proved it invincible and exposed their own weakness.

First the Jews made war on our Saviour's flock, and they were destroyed by their own weapon. For the good shepherd used the cross they had set up as a kind of club, and, as a shepherd does, drove them like wolves away from the sheep. After them came the worshippers of idols, who were put to shame by the champions of truth. After them came Simon and his disciples Menander and Cerdo; then Marcion and Valentinus; and after them Cerinthus and Saturninus, Basilides and Carpocrates, Marcus and Tatian, Montanus and Bardaisan, Artemon and Novatus, Sabellius and Nepos, Paul and Mani, Photinus and Marcellus; and those who came after them, Arius, Aetius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Maximus, Nestorius, that many-headed hydra Eutyches and Dioscorus, Zosimus, Apollinaris, Origen, Peter the wretched, Theodosius, Jacob, Julian, Zeno, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Cyrus, Macarius, Honorius, and the impious Muhammad, and any others who have slipped my memory, as happens to human beings. The day would fail me if I listed the names of the champions and leaders of impiety, whose very memory time has rightly blotted out. All of them alike, so to speak, made war on the apostolic preaching and were fittingly cast out of God's remembrance and out of the Church; and the Church, ever warred against and ever more victorious, lived in a state of peace.

After this the father of wickedness and inventor of evil, the devil, who never ceases to make war at every turn on man, created in God's image, saw that the Lord's flock easily overcame its open enemies. So — to go back to what I wrote earlier — he resolved to kindle the flame of war from within. He found an instrument worthy of his work: a man thought to work many wonders by sorcerous incantations and able to deceive those people who are dazzled by such things, a man who took both his descent and his way of thinking from the land of Syria. This beast with a lion's name, as I wrote before, was the first he stirred up against the spiritual veneration of the holy [icons]. Even when this man had been exposed as a manifest heretic by Germanus, champion of the truth, as was said earlier, the common enemy of mankind did not stop. When Leo too had broken off his life and become food for the undying worm and the eternal fire, the devil raised up in his place his foul offspring — Constantine, I mean — as one might say Ahab from Ahaz, or from Archelaus the more wicked Herod, the slave of adultery and murderer of the Forerunner. This tree, then, sprung from that wicked root, put forth

still more wicked fruit. He stored up every kind of deadly poison for his own soul, and he ravaged, overturned and burned every sight of the holy icons. Repulsed by the monks, the initiates of piety, he mustered war against them. He who was darkened in soul called the monastic habit "darkness," named those enrolled in it "the unmentionables," and called them idolaters because they venerated the revered icons. He assembled all the people under his rule and made them swear an oath, with the life-giving body and blood of Christ set before them, and the immaculate wood on which Christ our God stretched out his hands for us, and the holy and immaculate Gospels, in which Christ commands us not to swear at all. They swore that they had done these things and would speak against the power of the icons: that they would not venerate a holy icon but call it an idol; that they would not take communion from an abbot, or even greet one; and that if they found anyone at all who was an "unmentionable" clothed in darkness, they would revile him and stone him. What frivolity!

Then he found an instrument like himself in character and in sound — indeed of the same name and the same mind — from the ranks of the clergy, just as, to speak in the words of Scripture, Balak found Balaam and Jannes found Jambres. He brought him to the church, not by the vote of God and the priests but by his own villainy. Both went up onto the ambo, and from the hands of the emperor Constantine the unholy Constantine put on the foul double cloak — I mean the omophorion. He was unworthy of the P and more deserving of an F, for he appeared to the Church as a "phatriarch," a faction-leader, rather than a patriarch, while the tyrant himself was the first to cry out "Worthy!" What unworthiness! The shield-bearer became the installer of priests; the celebrant whose business was wars and murders, the man who had unlawfully taken three wives, was made the ordainer of priests. Who ever heard of such a thing since the world began, or saw it, or reported it? No one, truly. Nothing of the kind ever appeared even in the rites and sacrificial smoke of the Greeks. So it came to pass, in the prophet's words, "The people as the priest," and there was no one who consecrated or was consecrated.

Once that foul pair had been entwined like a lawless chain, edicts were sent out to every province, ordering the governors of each region to come to the imperial city with their bishops, so that a synod might be held against the holy and venerable icons. In every land and city one could see lament upon lament and woe upon woe from the pious; and from the impious, sacred things

outraged [?], vessels remade, and churches scraped and smeared with plaster because they had holy icons. Wherever there were venerable icons of Christ, or of the Mother of God, or of the saints, they were given over to fire, to scraping, or to being smeared over. But where there were pictures of trees or birds or brute beasts, and especially satanic horse-races, hunts, theatres and hippodromes, these were kept in honour and made to shine more brightly. Then one could truly say: "Woe is me, for the devout man has perished from the earth, and there is none upright among men." For with axe and hammer they broke down the doors of God's Church, and with fire they burned his sanctuary. The icon is called a door because it opens our mind, created after God, to the likeness of the prototype within. Gates that bear keys and seals indicate from the outside, through the security of their seals, what lies within. In the same way the representation in an icon, presenting its outlines as seals and its expressions as keys, points through material things to things perceived by the mind. And we do not worship the matter when we venerate it — far from it! — but through things perceived by the senses we reach out spiritually to their causes, as we do with the cross, the holy sanctuary, a saint's relic and everything else venerated in church. In this we fulfil that royal saying of Basil, who revealed heavenly things: that the honour paid to the image passes over to the prototype.

But let us return to our subject. While the Church of Christ was divided amid these painful events, the leading monks who held fast to piety — from the regions of Europe and Byzantium, from the provinces of Thynia and Bithynia, and the cave-dwellers and mountain-dwellers around Prusias — all came together to the mountain of the God-bearing Auxentius. They came to the all-blessed Stephen as to a guide and a watchman for their salvation, and begged him to become their counsellor in the way of salvation. They found him overwhelmed by dejection and tears over the innovating heresy, and they said to him: "Tell us, Father, what we should do. Our minds are weary and we are drowning in perplexity, for fear that human fear may betray the piety of the soul. For it is natural for the soul to fear death." The all-blessed man, seeing the great crowd of the Fathers, kissed their angelic grey hair and said: "Honoured Fathers and brothers, nothing is stronger than a will that chooses piety, and nothing more powerful than a soul that refuses to serve evil. I am convinced that both of these are preserved in your fatherly persons, and so it is rather you who should be my counsellors and pray for me. For my eyes have failed with tears

[?] over the ruin of the daughter of my people, I am compelled to cry out with Jeremiah, who both wrote these words and lived them. For I see the Bride of the Lord cruelly and bitterly besieged by the wicked, murderous, war-loving demon, who had a hand, through his image in human flesh, in what has befallen the Church of God. At the very creation he at once made war on our nature, and, begrudging us our life in paradise, brought it about that the divine law was set aside. Now he is again trying to destroy the precious body of the Church: he sets its members to rebel against one another, and he has stirred up among them a war without truce and without herald. Through the heresy he has whipped up among the crowd he has divided feet against one another, and hands, and eyes. You can see one eye eagerly leading toward the cliffs, while the other pulls the opposite way and points out the straight road. Of the feet, one obeys and follows the eye that sees crookedly; the other fights against it, boldly contradicts the one that leads it wrongly, and does not turn aside from the right path. Such is the battle that the enemy who sowed the tares has stirred up among the members of the Church. He exults and dances to see his own evil craft prevailing in this tyrant emperor. He revels in our misfortunes and gathers fuel from every side for the flames of war. He musters his own battle lines (I mean the children of the Greeks and of the Jews, and the Syrians, and the hordes of the heretics) and seats around us on every side a vast theatre, providing them with delight and pleasure from our sufferings. You can see those who sit in the gates prating against us, and those who drink wine singing songs about us. In their banquets and taverns, like pimps and lyre-singers, at the bidding of the cub they rehearse songs against us and mockingly foretell our doom. Therefore we, the precious sons of Zion, valued above gold, have been reckoned as earthen vessels, the work of the potter's hands. We have become a laughingstock to all the people, their song all day long. For the Lord in his anger has darkened the daughter of Zion. He has cast down from heaven to earth the glory of Israel and has not remembered his footstool in the day of his anger. For Jerusalem sinned grievously, and so she has been tossed about. Therefore my eyes run down with water, because the one who comforts me is far from me. And I cry to him who strikes and heals: "Have mercy on us, Lord, have mercy on us, for we have been filled with contempt; our soul is filled with it more than enough. Take away the reproach and give it to our enemies who now prosper, and the contempt to the arrogant—

[?] your flock, which bears your name, calling us idolaters and calling your church a temple of idols. But renew us like the early dawn. Let your faithfulness be multiplied every morning, for our groans are many and our heart has fainted. You have broken down our hedge, and all who pass along the road pluck our fruit. The boar from the forest has ravaged us, this cub born of a lion, and like a wild solitary beast he has devoured us. O Lord, God of hosts, turn back now and look upon this vine, and restore the vine that your right hand planted, and look upon the Son of Man whom you made strong for yourself." But while I was weeping, lamenting and supplicating because of the mist that lies over both shepherds and flock, which has given free rein to wolves and thieves, and while I was begging my God to scatter the gloom and to restore the former ray of Orthodoxy and the spiritual veneration of the holy and revered icons, I forgot my promise and drew out the lament. Only now have I remembered it, finding in the prayer "the Son of Man whom you made strong for yourself." Through him you accomplished our salvation, O Maker of [?], whose divine form in the flesh these babblers have handed over to fire and to scraping away. But may the Lord consume them in fire, and may their memory be scraped from the earth, together with all who trust in them, for he is a God of vengeance and will not pass over in silence the capture of his Church.

Our all-blessed Father Stephen spoke these words to that holy company of monks. While all were shedding tears and beating their breasts, the Father groaned from the depths and said: "There are three regions in our part of the world that have not shared in this foul heresy, and I advise you to flee to them. For no other place under the dragon's power is left that has not obeyed his empty babble." They asked, "And where are these regions, Father?" He at once [replied]: "Those on the upper side of the Black Sea, lying toward the province of Zichia, from Bosporus, Cherson and Nicopsis, and those extending toward the Gothic Hollow. Then those lying toward the Parthenian Sea, where the southern gulf is sailed, on the way down toward elder Rome: the metropolis of the Nicopolitans, Naples, and the lands lying as far as the Tiber, the river of Rome. Also the coastlands of the province of Lycia, from Syllaeum and Syke, and the places reached by sailing along the Propontis itself, and the island of Cyprus and the coast opposite, as far as Tripoli, Tyre and Joppa. And what need is there to speak of the presiding bishops of Rome and Antioch, Jerusalem and Alexandria? They not only abhorred and anathematized the abominable doctrine of the Icon-burners, but they have also not

ceased to heap insults in denunciatory letters on the impious emperor who assented to it, calling him an apostate and a heresiarch. Among them the most honoured and most wise John of Damascus, the priest, whom this tyrant calls Mansur but whom we call holy and God-bearing, has not ceased writing to him and calling him a scoffer and a Mamed, an icon-burner and a hater of saints, and calling the bishops under him not bishops but benighters, slaves of the belly whose minds are on their stomachs. Above all he called those lovers of the hippodrome races and the shows, Pastillas and Tricaccabus, Nicolaites and the demon-loving Atzypius, new Orebs, Zeebs, Zebahs and Zalmunnas, and new Dathans, and those under them the congregation of Abiram."

When the all-blessed Stephen had said these things, and many others profitable for the soul, the Fathers offered a mournful prayer, embraced the saint in a last farewell, and left for the places that offered the safest refuge. They went not because they were cowards who feared martyrdom, but because they dreaded the tyrant's cunning and their own lack of trial. For what is untried is not proven, while what has been tested in deeds is more surely proven, like gold in a furnace. One could see Byzantium being stripped, as if by captivity, of the monastic ranks and of the Nazirite habit. One sailed off to the Black Sea, another reached Cyprus, another planned to set out for Rome. Thus, exiled from their own monasteries, they became known as strangers and sojourners.

The tyrant scraped bare the venerable church of the all-immaculate Theotokos at Blachernae. Its walls had formerly been adorned with painted images running from God's condescension to us, through all kinds of miracles, up to his ascension and the descent of the Holy Spirit. Having thus removed all the mysteries of Christ, he made the church a fruit-store and an aviary. He decorated it all round with mosaics of trees and all kinds of birds and beasts, and other things set in circles of ivy leaves, with cranes, crows and peacocks, and so, if I may put it so, he left it truly unadorned. If any who share his opinions suppose that I am slandering him, let them go to this church, and, convinced that these things are true, let them say with David the holy psalmist: "O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have made your Church, the spiritual Jerusalem, into a fruit-store; they have given the flesh of your holy ones, the precious relics of your martyrs and monks, to the beasts of the earth, to the fire and to the depths of the sea." In this all-venerable church, then, the villain presided, together with the namesake betrayer of Christ's flock and the belly-slave bishops under him,

and they held their abominable synod, hostile to God, calling the revered icons idols and statues. My bones shudder and my inmost parts feel it, as Eliphaz says, O wise and faithful audience, whenever I merely call to mind what was done then. Next, those estranged from God anathematized Germanus, the divine presiding bishop of the Church who rightly divided the word of truth, and called him a worshipper of wood. O the hardness of the enemy! O the blasphemy! O the perversion! How shall I grasp, my Christ, your boundless forbearance at that time? They uttered a great many blasphemies and attacked the saints and the immaculate Theotokos, claiming that she could not help anyone after death. Then came the last, the first and the worst of all. Those foul and unholy men, the lawless Babylonians who ruined Christ's vineyard, of whom it is written, "Lawlessness went out from the priests of Babylon," and, "Many shepherds have ruined my vineyard and defiled my portion"; who, as the proverb says, strayed from the paths of their own field and gathered fruitlessness in their hands; who made no distinction between holy and profane, but wrought lamentation and woe between the altar [?]: these men rose from where they sat together with all the people, lifted their hands on high, and shouted that pitiful cry: "Today salvation has come to the world, for you, O emperor, have redeemed us from idols!" O wicked cry! As it boomed out it darkened heaven, shook the earth and defiled the air, and it made all who shouted it strangers to God. For if this prime author of impiety is the cause of the destruction of idols, then Christ became man in vain, and the teaching of the apostles is empty. And if, as you say, it is he who redeemed us from the worship of creatures and the curse of idols, he whom you even call the thirteenth apostle, and not Christ, then, in the words of Paul, the herald of God, you were not baptized into the Trinity at all. You were baptized instead (to answer your arrogant folly with something laughable) into Pastillas, Tricaccabus and Caballas, his teachers and yours. The memory, the doctrine and the very names of these three the supremely luminous and venerable Trinity has blotted out of that same Church.

But let us leave these trifles, since time presses, and set out now and proceed. Let us return to our subject and rejoin the all-blessed Stephen. When these things had been done in this way, and every hand had signed and every mouth confessed, the tyrant learned about our holy father Stephen. He summoned one of his illustrious magnates, a most learned man, skilled in both speaking and listening, named Callistus, who had been honoured with the rank of patrician and who, moreover,

had been schooled to the utmost in the emperor's heresy. He sent him off with these words: "Go to the hill of Auxentius. There a man named Stephen lurks in his den, [?] of the swarm of the unmentionables. Persuade him to sign at the synod, and say: 'Out of friendship for you, because of the piety of your life, our pious and orthodox emperors Constantine and Leo command you to sign the definition of our orthodox synod.'" He gave him dates and dried figs and other things suitable as food for an ascetic, for even the tyrant knew of the saint's austere way of life, which drew near to God. Callistus went straight to the mountain, presented himself at the summit of the hill, and delivered the message to the holy Father by word of mouth, advising him [?] to sign and to approve the emperors' definition.

But this honourable Stephen, a rival of the first Stephen, who always saw the Lord at his right hand and was not shaken by any heretical notion, said to the patrician: "Take note, my lord patrician: since a heretical opinion has been set out in the definition of this sham assembly of a synod, Stephen will neither sign nor call bitter sweet, lest I bring upon myself the prophet's 'woe.' Moreover, for the veneration of the holy icons I am ready to die gladly, and I take no account of the heresiarch emperor who dares to reject them." He cupped his palm by bringing his fingers together in the ordinary way and held it out, saying: "Even if my life-blood is only this much, let it be poured out for the icon of Christ. And take back the food he sent. Let not the oil of a sinner anoint my head, and let not my throat be sweetened by a heretic's food." When the official heard this, he went back, reached the palace, and reported everything to the man who had sent him.

The emperor at once gnashed his teeth in rage like a lion and let out no small roar from his wrathful soul. He immediately dispatched chief satraps and vigorous shield-bearers, together with the patrician Callistus whom he had sent before, to go to the mountain. He ordered them to drag the saint from his cell in anger and keep him under guard in the lower monastery until he should decide what to do with him. They reached the mountain and arrived at the monastery. Leaping like wild beasts, they kicked at the doors, burst murderously into the holy cave, and dragged the saint out as though from some spiritual bridal chamber. Because of his extreme austerity and his very cramped dwelling, his shins had become fixed against his thighs, and he could neither stand nor move. When those shield-bearers saw the Father's remarkable state, they felt great compassion

for the saint because of the astonishing sight. Two of them joined together, put the saint's arms over their shoulders and supported his knees with their hands, and in this way they reached the cemetery of St Auxentius. There they shut up the saint with the company of monks who were with him, a company upheld by God, while they themselves sat in front of the doors awaiting the emperor's decision. The all-blessed one, inside with his company, did not stop chanting clearly: "We venerate your immaculate icon, O Good One," and the rest; and after that the Glory: "I fell among the robbers of my own thoughts, and I, wretch that I am, was robbed of my mind," and the rest of the hymn. When the guards in front of the doors heard them singing this, they shook their heads and lamented to one another, saying: "Woe to us, for monks, men who have done no wrong and are being ill-treated, rightly proclaim us robbers."

Six days passed, and those shut in with the saint remained without food. On the seventh day another official arrived from the tyrant emperor to restore the saint to his own monastery, since a war against the Scythians was at hand. But that most wicked Callistus, so ill-suited to his name, took one of the saint's disciples aside, gave him gold and promised him more, and persuaded that wretch to become a second Judas and take up arms against his teacher. This disciple's name was Sergius. The troops asked the saint for a prayer, went to the imperial city, and marched with the emperor into Europe against the Scythians. That son of lawlessness, Sergius, the second Iscariot and heir of the noose, had wholly put on Satan through the treacherous gold, and from then on he never stopped plotting in secret against the venerable Father. When he saw that he could not achieve his aim, he left that holy fold and ran to the chief tax-collector of the gulf of Nicomedia, surnamed Aulikalamos. He gained him as an accomplice and partner in his own perdition, and together they composed a document full of invented slanders against the holy Stephen, in which they wrote: "First and foremost, he anathematizes your memory as that of a heretic, and calls you Syrian-born and Vitalis [?], and digs pits against you as he sits on the mountain." They slandered him with many other things besides, which are not worth mentioning or setting down in writing. "And," it says, "he seduced a certain noblewoman, tonsured her, and keeps her in the lower monastery, and at night she goes up to him on the hill for passionate and sinful intercourse." Now this woman, most faithful

hearers, is the one mentioned earlier, who had disposed of all her possessions well and had become the saint's spiritual daughter by receiving the holy habit. They led her maidservant astray, arranged to free her and to marry her to a man of the palace, and so taught her to say what they wanted against her mistress and the saint. The devil's pair put together this deceitful, forged document and sent it by courier to the emperor among the Scythians, to be placed in his hands.

He read it and lawlessly condemned the saint, and, as if seizing a convenient opportunity, he promptly sent couriers to the man governing the city in his place, a man named Anthes who held the rank of patrician. He gave him orders in a letter that ran as follows: "We have been fully assured in many ways, by events themselves, that you are well disposed toward our orders, and for this reason we have entrusted you with the dignity of acting in our stead. For like a star you keep your eyes sleepless for our repose, and rightly so, as a faithful friend and a grateful servant. Therefore, since you are capable and loyal to us in both respects, we order you to go at once to the monastery at the foot of the hill of Auxentius, where women live who are harlots pretending to be pious, of the roll of the unmentionables. Seize one of them named Anna, send her to us by these same couriers, and present her quickly at the camp. Farewell."

The servant, more lawless than his lawless emperor, did not even finish reading the letter, but at once fell upon the monastery like a barbarian with a crowd of soldiers. He found those holy women performing the doxology to God at the third hour. Bursting into the church like stallions mad for mares, they terrified the virgins of Christ, baring their swords like robbers and whirling them through the air [?]. In the uproar the hymnody fell silent, and one could see the women of God lamenting. One fled inside the holy railing into the sanctuary; another lifted the holy altar-cloth and [hid] under the holy table; another made for the mountain and ran from the hands of the impious. When the honourable old woman who was superior of the monastery learned of this foul attack (she was living in stillness in a cell), she came out to them, calm in soul, and said: "O Christians, if you have any hope in God, why are you carrying out the exploits of godless barbarians?" Astonished at that holy woman's boldness, and learning that she was the superior, they dropped their brutality and quietly answered: "Hand over to us Anna, Stephen's friend, because the emperor needs her at the camp." She called her by name, and with her another named Theophano, and said to them: "Go, precious children, to the emperor, and [?]"

[?] … and give him your answers sensibly, so that he does not lead you astray. Go in peace, go, and may the Lord be with you." Those honourable women took up their scapulars, made the customary prostration, received the blessing of that honourable abbess, and left the monastery. They were dragged off and brought to the emperor in the army camp. O the ready obedience of nuns under rule, and O the most pure prayer of a faithful mother! When they had been brought into the camp and their case had been made known to the emperor, he ordered them to be separated from each other. He summoned the woman who was being sought, the spiritual daughter of Saint Stephen, and said to her: "I am convinced that what has been told us about you is true. For I know how easily a woman's mind is taken captive. Tell me, then, how did this sorcerer persuade you to abandon your parents' high standing and take up this darkened habit? Or is it, as I have heard, that he simply wants to fornicate with you? What sort of beauty of his was it that deceived you?" When that honourable woman heard these shameful words, she, like the chaste Susanna, forgot the weakness of her sex and answered him with good sense: "Emperor, my body lies before you. Punish it, slaughter it, do whatever you will and wish with me. For from Anna you will hear nothing but the truth. I do not know the man as you describe him. But as I do know him, I will tell you: I know him to be holy and righteous, a teacher who profits souls, and the guide of my salvation." The tyrant was struck dumb at the woman's boldness. He bit the fingertip of one hand, twirled the other in the air [?], whistled, and sat there frowning, and remained speechless. For this was the abominable emperor's habit every time. Then he ordered her to be kept under guard, and the sister who was with her to be sent back, against her will, to her own monastery. When she reached her own monastery, she made known everything that had happened to the abbess and the sisters [?] … and she went up the hill to our divinely inspired Father Stephen and begged the saint to pray for her, especially since her struggle was on his account. The emperor broke up the army camp, and when he reached the imperial city, he ordered the saint's spiritual daughter to be kept in fetters in the pitch-dark prison of the Phiale, since he wished to interrogate her [again?].
