Around the evening hours he sent her the following message by a eunuch whose rank is called cubicularius:

"Spare yourself, woman, and live well with the empress. Put off this garment of darkness, and tomorrow tell the truth about Stephen before all the people. For look, your own servant girl is also exposing the truth. If you will not do this, but keep up your stony-hearted disobedience and go on lying, I will set your flesh before your eyes limb by limb. But if, on the other hand, you do what I want and confess his adulteries and fornications, I will count you worthy of many honours and gifts." When the honourable woman heard this, she groaned in pain from the depths of her heart, shook her head, and said to him: "Go away from me, man, go away. Let the will of the Lord be done." At dawn the emperor gathered a crowd of people in front of the [?] of the Phiale. Thinking he could persuade her, he ordered her to stand naked in the midst of them all. He set a heap of ox-hide whips before her eyes and said: "I will wear all these out on your back and your belly unless you bring Stephen's foul fornications with you into the open." When the honourable woman made no answer, the tyrant snorted with rage, called her an adulteress, and ordered her to be flogged. At once eight strong men took hold of both her hands and stretched her out in the air in the shape of a cross. One stood at her belly and one at her back, and they beat her without mercy. She said nothing except, "I do not know the man as you describe him," and, "Lord, have mercy." The tyrant also set that treacherous slave girl of hers opposite her, to accuse her in front of everyone just as he had coached her. She accused her on oath, raised her hands against her mistress, and drenched her lady's face with spit. Then the tyrant's fellow initiates in impiety kept sounding in her ears that she should say what would most please the emperor and so live. She answered them with the same words as before. When the tyrant saw that the merciless beating had already left her without a voice, he thought she had died. He got up and went back into the palace in shame, after ordering her to be thrown into one of the monasteries of Byzantium and left without care. But he did not stop scheming how he might [?] the saint by any means.

The next day he summoned one of his lusty young men, whom he swore he loved dearly, named George, surnamed Synkletos. He said to him in private (as George himself declared on oath when he was dying, to those who reported it to me): "How great, George, is your love for me?" He said: "Boundless, master, and beyond all reckoning." The emperor said to him again: "And would you readily die for love of me?" He bowed to the ground, crossed his hands on his breast, and swore with all eagerness that he would die for him. The emperor embraced him: "See, a new Isaac too!" [?] And

he said to him: "I am not asking you to die for me, nor even to lose a single limb. I beg this one thing of you, as a father: go to the hill of Auxentius and persuade the unmentionable one who lurks there to count you among those under him and give you the same habit. If you succeed in this, come back to us as fast as you can." That son and servant of lawlessness received the word with joy. After he had been taught a great many tricks of villainy, he hurried off to become a morsel for the dragon. He went up the mountain and hid in a wooded place of wild brushwood. Around midnight he came out of that thicket and reached the monastery. He stood at the gate and raised mournful cries like these: "Have pity on me, you Christians who live in this place, or I will become food for wild beasts or be sent over the cliff! For I have lost my way." He burst out with other pleading words as well, lamenting like the devil he was. Our all-blessed Father Stephen heard the mournful, wailing voice. He called the Marinus mentioned before, who was upheld by God, and ordered him to bring the man who was lamenting in to him. He came in, made a prostration to the ground, and said, "Bless me, Father." The saint blessed him and raised him up. He recognized what he was from his clothing [?] and his face, and above all from his beard. For it had been shaved down to the skin of his face, in keeping with the tyrant's own decree. God had commanded Moses to tell all the people, "You shall not pluck [?] the hair of your beard, so as not to make yourselves a lock." But this new Jebusite and Amalekite set himself against God's command and against Moses, and decreed the opposite. Everyone, from the aged and those with the whitest hair down to elders and young men, was to have his beard shaved down to the skin of the face, so that they would look beardless and be lusty at all times, like stallions mad for mares. Even to this day some among us who are not truly ours (for they enter our fold in habit, not in manner of life) are past seventy, more or less, and still do the same thing with their beards. May the Lord correct them and pull them free from the mind, memory and faith of that tyrant, and make them firm in the truth before they suffer the death of both body and soul. But to return to our all-blessed Father Stephen, if I have digressed a little, compelled by necessity: when he saw young George in such a guise, he said: "Surely, brother, you are from the imperial palace?" He said to him: "Yes, Father. But through the lawlessness of the emperor who rules so impiously we have all turned Jew and veered into danger to our souls. I have barely come to my senses at last from this most evil

way of life, and see, I have been guided by God to come here. And now, honourable Father, do not banish me from your soul-saving community. Let me receive the angelic habit." The honourable Stephen said to him: "I cannot do this because of the danger that hangs over us from the tyrant. He may learn of it, carry your soul off into slavery away from salvation, and tangle it again in the old snares." He fell down again and begged him: "You will answer to God for me if you put off tonsuring me." The saint said to him again: "If there were no danger, I would fulfil the word of the Gospel: 'Anyone who comes to me I will never cast out.' But since, as you say, you come with your whole heart, I will fulfil it. Only see to it that temptation does not overtake you." With these words he stripped him of his worldly clothing and put on him the garment of obedience, and he kept him so for three days. Meanwhile the tyrant gathered the people in the theatre of the hippodrome, at the steps in the place called that of the Reds. He stood above them and cried out: "I can have no share of life alongside the God-hated swarm of the unmentionables!" The people cried out and began to make an uproar, saying, "Not a trace of their habit is to be seen in your city, master!" He shouted back in anger: "I can no longer endure their plots. They have drawn away all who are under me and handed them over to darkness. And not content with that, look, they have even snatched from my side the one my soul loves, George Synkletos I mean, and made him a [monk?]. O the violence of their scheming! But let us cast our care upon the Lord, and he will soon bring him to light. Only let us pray." They all said: "Truly your heart is in the hand of God, and when you pray the Lord will surely hear you." After the third day the most honourable Stephen gave much instruction to George, who was so crafty in wickedness, tonsured him, and clothed him in the holy habit. But that servant of lawlessness kept none of the things of God (for, as it is written, "Wisdom will not enter a malicious soul"). After another three days he fled from the hill and went off to the palace. The emperor welcomed him gladly, as the one who had carried out the design of his own scheme, and kissed him, not because of the habit but because of the transgression. Since he had found a pretext to kill the saint, and had seized the opportune moment, he ordered people of every age to assemble at dawn in the theatre of the hippodrome: the old, elders and young men, adolescents and newborn infants, men and women together, as at a convened silention. [Variant readings: "blows"; "of the soul"; "having done." (14) Steps [?]]

So when everyone, so to speak, had gathered, and a countless multitude was packed together so tightly that they were choking one another, the tyrant took his stand again on the same steps and cried out: "My fortune has won, and God has heard my prayers!" The people shouted, "And when has your God ever failed to hear you?" He was delighted, laughed loudly, and said: "The Lord has revealed to me the one I was seeking. If you wish, I will show him to you." The crowd roared with a rushing noise: "Punish him, slaughter him, burn him with fire for transgressing your command!" The emperor brought him out for all to see. When that endless, stirred-up mob saw him in the monastic habit, they broke out in that pitiable cry, like the Jews who once cried, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" against the Son of God. So these too cried: "Evil to see! Evil years! Let him be killed, let him be killed!" Then at the tyrant's command they stripped him of his holy scapular and flung it at the people, and it was trampled underfoot, and likewise the holy cowl. When they took off the analabos bearing the figure of the cross, to fling it too, the emperor took it in his hands, turned it this way and that, and asked, "What could this be?" One of the wicked officials, a man like Satan in his ways, whose name I will pass over (for his surname is a dragon's), shouted out: "Throw that too, emperor, to be trampled: the rope of the satanic noose!" So he threw it too, and they trampled the [?] strap. Then four men bent to the ground, took hold of the apostate's garments, [?] him, and set him naked in the midst of everyone, as if he had been flayed. They brought a jar full of water and poured it over him from his head down, as a reversal of baptism, so to speak. Then they tied a helmet on him and put a soldier's uniform on him. With his own hands the tyrant hung a sword from his shoulders, promoted him in rank, and enrolled him in the dignity of strator. At once he ordered a countless sword-bearing multitude to seize the hill of Saint Auxentius. The whole multitude ran straight there, scattered the saint's disciples, and set fire to the monastery and the church, reducing them to dust down to the ground. They took the saint out of his cave and headed down towards the sea. What words and what lament could tell in full the athlete's sufferings that the saint endured on that journey? Some beat him on the loins with rods [?]; others, down the slope of the ravine, [variant: "stratorikion," for so it reads there [?]]

shoved him along; others threw him into thorny plants [?]. Since, as was said before, he could not walk because of his extreme confinement and abstinence, they put him in a boat [?] and sailed along the coast, and reached the holy monastery of Philippicus, which lies by the sea at the town of Chrysopolis. There they shut the saint up and reported his case to the emperor. When the emperor learned of the dragging away like a captive, in disgrace, and the complete destruction of the monastery, he issued a decree: if anyone were caught approaching the hill of Auxentius, he would suffer punishment by the sword. Then he summoned the heresiarchs who shared his nonsense, bishops of darkness, if I may put it so: Theodosius, falsely called bishop of Ephesus; Constantine, the innovator of Nicomedia; his namesake of Nacolia; Sisinnius Pastillas; and Basil Tricaccabus. He summoned also the leading men of the palace: the Callistus mentioned before, Combocono the secretary, and Masaras, who had the mind of a Saracen. He sent them to his own namesake and kindred spirit, the chief shepherd, so that he might make the journey with them to the monastery at Chrysopolis mentioned above. But that hireling shepherd and traitor, who knew from experience the learning and orthodoxy of our holy and most blessed Father Stephen, refused to go with them, saying: "Go in peace, go. Between Constantine and Stephen, when it comes to debating, there is a great gulf. I have words and nothing more, but he has, along with words, the power of the divine Spirit. You will see what you hear from him." So they took the definition of the pseudo-synod with them, set out from the patriarchate, and reached the monastery. They went in and prayed in the holy church, then withdrew to the fountain, sat down on the steps there, and ordered at once

that the saint be brought. The saint was brought, held up by two men, because, as was said before, he could not walk, and his feet were locked in iron fetters. When these God-haters saw this, they wept. Then Theodosius of Ephesus said to him: "Man of God, how have you come to suspect us of heresy, and to set yourself above emperors and archbishops and bishops and all Christians? Are all of us really working the ruin of our own souls?" The saint said to them in a quiet voice: "Pay attention to what is written in Elijah the prophet, to Ahab: 'It is not I who trouble Israel, but you and your father's house.' For it is not I who am perverting things, but you, who have transgressed the teaching handed down from the Fathers of long ago and brought new empty babble into the Church. For if, as a wise man said, what excels in antiquity is venerable, then the novelties you have uttered are all spurious and alien to God, and counterfeits of the Church besides. Indeed, one may say in the words of the prophet: The kings of the earth and the rulers, together with the shepherds and the betrayers of the flock, have gathered together against the Church of Christ, devising empty and vain things." When the saint had said this, Constantine of Nicomedia, who was young in body and lusty in mind (he was then at the height of his youth, about thirty years old), leapt up and tried to kick the saint in the face as he sat on the ground, as was once done to the holy Eleazar under Antiochus. And one of the bitter and savage guards leapt at him and kicked him in the flanks, so that he fell and had to pick himself up. But the honourable Stephen, holding fast to the commandment of the Gospel, made himself ready to take blows not only on one cheek but on the other as well. Callistus, Combocono and the other members of the senate silenced the unholy Constantine and said to the saint: "Two options lie before you: either be persuaded and sign, or else be handed over to death for speaking against the law of the Fathers and of emperors taught by God." The saint said: "Pay attention, my lord patrician. For me to live is Christ, and to die for his holy image is gain and glory. Once and twice I have told you, tripping the wrestler [?]: if there is so much life-blood in me, let it be poured out for such a cause. But let the definition of your synod be read, and let me see what just argument it brings for the destruction of the divine and venerable icons."

At once Constantine of Nacolia opened the tome and said: "Definition of the holy and ecumenical seventh synod." The saint motioned to him with his hand to be silent and said: "O what folly! You began from a lie, took the [?] of innovating empty babble as your shield, and ended in a lie, you accusers of Christians. How can a synod be holy that profaned holy things? Were not holy things [?] by you? Was not a charge brought in your synod by Christ-loving men against a bishop who had trampled on a holy paten of the immaculate mysteries of God because venerable images of Christ, of his Mother and of the Forerunner were engraved on it? Yet you set the charge of trampling above the images, admitted him to celebrate the liturgy, and excommunicated the Christ-loving men, calling them avengers of idols. What could be more hateful to holiness than this? Did you not [tear down?] the sacred veils and bring them to destruction? How then can your synod be called holy? Did you not strip the title 'holy' from all the saints, the righteous, the apostles and the martyrs, and decree that people should say: 'Where are you going?' 'To the Apostles.' 'Where have you come from?' 'From the Forty Martyrs.' 'And where are you going?' 'To the martyr Theodore, and to the martyr Acacius, and to those like them.' Are these not your teachings? And how could those who profaned holy things convene a holy synod? O the shamelessness! And how can it be ecumenical, when the bishop of Rome did not consent to it, although there is a canon that church affairs are not to be regulated without the Pope of Rome; nor did the bishop of Alexandria, so to speak, nor of Antioch, nor of Jerusalem? Where are their letters of assent, that your pseudo-synod should be proclaimed ecumenical? And how can it be seventh, when it did not follow the six before it? For every seventh follows the first and the second, the third, the fourth and the fifth, and the seventh comes after the sixth. But you set aside the traditions of the six, and I am at a loss to know how you named it the seventh synod." When Tricaccabus said, "And what have we set aside of the six holy ecumenical synods?" the saint said: "Were not those six synods assembled in sacred churches? The first at Nicaea, in the church of Holy Wisdom; the second at Constantinople, in the church of Holy Peace; the third at Ephesus, in the church of the Theologian; the fourth in our own metropolis of the Chalcedonians, in the shrine of the All-Praised; the fifth again at Constantinople; and the sixth, partly in the church of Holy Wisdom and partly in the sacred palace, at the place called the Trullus, which we call the Oaton? And in all these very churches," he said, "was the icon not received and venerated? Tell me, bishop." When he said that it was so, the righteous man [lifted?] his eyes to heaven

…raising [?], he groaned deeply from his heart, stretched out his hands and said: “If anyone does not venerate our Lord Jesus Christ depicted in an icon, circumscribed according to his humanity, let him be anathema, and let him be counted with those who cried out, ‘Away with him, away with him, crucify him!’” These babblers were astounded at the saint's boldness. While he still wanted to go on speaking, they got up, ordered only that he be locked up, and went back to the palace in shame. When the emperor asked, “Well, what did you accomplish?”, the bishops still wanted to hide their defeat, but Callistus and his party answered, “We are beaten, emperor, we are beaten. The man is far above us in power, in argument and in his boldness in the face of death.” The emperor boiled over with rage and at once wrote out an order exiling him to the far side of the Hellespont, to the island called Proconnesus. The saint spent seventeen days in the monastery of Chrysopolis and remained without food the whole time. The emperor sent him a great deal for his sustenance, but he sent it all back, repeating the saying recorded earlier. In those days the abbot of the monastery fell gravely ill, and the doctors gave up hope for him because of a burning fever. Seeing himself entirely spent, he sent the leading monks of the monastery as envoys to the saint, where he was confined, and begged him either to come to him or at least to pray for him. He said: “We are being separated from one another in body. But come, honored Father, if only so that my weak and humble self may embrace you. For my strength will scarcely [?] my soul until the ninth hour.” When the saint heard this, he was eager to go. He found the sick man, took hold of his wrist and said: “May the physician of our souls and bodies, who took up our infirmities and bore our diseases, visit you with his healing power and raise you up.” At once the fever abated. Then the saint said, “Don't you feel like having some undiluted wine?” He answered, “Yes, Father.” The honored Stephen filled his own flask with undiluted wine and gave it to the abbot to drink. As soon as he drank it he broke into a heavy sweat, and the crisis of the illness turned him toward health. The saint took his leave and said to him: “Pray for me, and remember my lowliness, if you should ever need to go up to the mountain.” And so he left there and set his course out to sea. He boarded the ship and reached the island of his exile already mentioned. He was put ashore there, and passing through its more deserted parts he came to a place that was steep

and frightening, above the sea. Because he loved stillness, he went around the cliffs that overhang the shore, and as though guided by God he found a cave-like dwelling, very pleasant and wonderful, in the southern cliff of the island. It was called Kissoudas, and in it stood a most venerable church of Anne, the ancestress of God. The blessed man was overjoyed, as though God had prepared the place for him, and he settled there, living on whatever herbs he came across. The saint's disciples, who had been driven from the mountain, heard of their master's exile and together made their way to Proconnesus. They went to the saint like sheep gathering at the shepherd's whistle. Only two of that holy company had been carried off captive and had taken up secular dress. One was Sergius, mentioned above, who had also written that slanderous paper against the saint and sent it to the emperor in the army camp. The other was Stephen, wretched in soul, who had been an attendant of the often-mentioned Callistus; he had received the holy habit from the saint and had been made a monk and priest of the monastery on the mountain. This wretched Stephen was carried off together with Sergius and cast himself away from God and from the habit. The emperor clothed him in secular dress, and returning like a dog to its own vomit he said: “Today, master, through you I have been snatched from the jaws of Satan and have put on the light.” The tyrant was charmed by these pitiable words and took him up because of his gluttony and his betrayal of God and of the habit. He appointed him officiant in his own palace called Sophianai, where he also held his abominable processions, and nicknamed him “Papas of Joy.” Only these two fell away, as Judas once did from the twelve apostles, and as the one who broke away from the forty martyrs and fell. All the other brothers were again shepherded by him and founded a monastery on Proconnesus. The saint's mother, too, left the monastery of Trichinaraia together with his sister, reached the island and visited the saint. The saint built a small pillar-like cell in that place, which survives to this day, and he enclosed himself in it in the forty-ninth year of his age, keeping to the regimen of his former austerity. Now it is time for me to spread my narrative over the meadow of his miracles on the island, so far as I am able, so that in this way we may join the lovers of God and of feasts in celebrating, and say: Truly wonderful in his saints

is God. Let no one disbelieve, brothers, especially since the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these”, not drawing the benefit from his own power, but from my name and from calling on me. For I am the one who works all things in all by my sovereign authority. So it was with our great Father Stephen, truly a man of God, honorable in soul and body. He longed for a life without possessions and kept only the icon of Christ and of his Mother as his safeguard. He was rich toward God and was counted worthy of precious grace. At once he received authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the evil enemy, and to heal every disease and every infirmity, and he showed us the marvels of the wonder-working God, his abundant grace, his gushing spring, his honey-sweet streams. Once a blind man, like the man born blind, fell down before this blessed Stephen on the island, crying out: “Servant of the Most High God, Stephen, heal my eyes, open my blindness and give light to me who am in darkness, so that through you I may see the harmony and order of visible things, marvel at their excellence, and praise the Creator through his creatures.” The blessed Stephen saw that he was terribly darkened by gloom into blindness, yet had the faith that moves mountains, and he answered him: “Why do you come to me, young man, asking me to give you what is beyond me? What virtue have you seen in me, my friend, that you ask to receive this healing from me, when only the Creator and God of all bestows it, where and when and on whom he wills? Why did you not run to him? Why have you left the Creator and come to the creature? Why have you abandoned the Master and come to the servant? Do you not know that all of us alike need his help? Do you not know that I too am a man like you? Why then do you seek what I cannot possess? Why do you want me to become the healer of such an illness, when he alone has the power to grant its cure, he who healed the blind man long ago?” With these words the holy man was gently trying to put the young man off, driving him away, as it were, with kind words. But he persisted, and imitating the blind man of old, he cried out loudly and implored him: “Have mercy on me, true servant of God, Stephen! For he has granted you this grace, and through you the true Light will grant my eyes their brightness. Do not blunt your boldness with hesitation, blessed one, do not put off the gift by delay, do not cover the sun with a cloud. See my affliction and grant the healing; measure my

faith and give the grace; weigh my longing and heal my suffering.” What then did the honored Stephen do? “Do you have faith?” he said. “Do you venerate the icon of Christ and of his Mother and of the saints? Do you believe in God, who heals even through icons? Just as,” he said, “long ago that dishonored Mary of Egypt believed, received a pledge from the icon, came to repentance and was saved?” The young man answered: “I believe, Lord, and believing I come forward and venerate.” Then the saint said to him: “In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, who healed the blind man, in whom you believed when you came here, and whom you have confessed that you venerate as circumscribed in an icon according to the flesh: see the sun, with nothing to hinder you.” At once his eyes were opened, and the young man was made well,

[?] the healing, he went away glad and rejoicing, praising God and glorifying him who grants his saints such gifts against diseases. This was the holy man's first miracle on the island, the firstfruits of his labors. Having worthily praised Christ, its giver, and the holy man, let us pass on to another of his miracles. A woman of some standing who lived in Cyzicus had a child about nine years old who was possessed by a demon. When she heard about the saint, she made her way to the island with the child. As soon as the afflicted child saw the cell from a distance, it was stirred up by the demon and was tossed up again and again, hanging in the air, stretched out, and then suddenly hurled down. It uttered frequent, inarticulate cries at the saint, as happens when the demon has taken over the possessed person and it is he who does all the speaking, using the sufferer's body as his own instrument. His mother, in more pain than the sufferer, weeping and beating her breast and holding the child by the hand, cried out: “Have mercy on me, saint, utterly wretched as I am! I have only one child in this life, and you see him now possessed by a demon. If I pray to God that he should die, childlessness wounds me; yet I cannot bear to have him possessed. Night and day he is out of his mind and grieves my soul. Have mercy on two souls and heal them, saint: him from the demon, and me from grief.” And such sorrowful things as befall mothers when a beloved child suffers [?]

[?]. The blessed Stephen was moved with compassion and told one of the monks to seal the child's whole body with the sign of the cross, while he himself prayed from his cell with tears. When after the prayer the child was convulsed, he called the boy by name, had him venerate the icon of Christ, and sent him home healthy with his mother. Plainly fulfilled in them was that saying of David, about a mother going on her way rejoicing over her child. Another woman, a most respectable one, had suffered from a flow of blood for seven years. She was wasting away from the flow of blood and was ashamed; now alone [?], she did not know what to do, having by now given up hope of healing because of the length of time. She lived in Heraclea in Thrace near the shore, and when she heard from those who sailed there about the holy man's miracles, she began asking, pleading and begging: “Where does the friend of God, and my physician, live?” People pointed across the water and showed her the island and the place. Putting aside all hesitation, she boarded a small boat, sailed quickly to the island and hurried to the holy man's place of healing. She showed him her ailment, told him how long it had lasted, and with lamentation and tears begged to be healed. [?] The Father prayed and healed her by the seal in Christ and by the veneration of his icon. She grew strong in body, and on the third day the woman found her constitution whole and truly strong, in no way divided or drained by the illness. But my account leads me from one thing to another and does not let me be silent even when I wish to be. Indeed, I confessed at the outset that my poor understanding is not equal to completing these narratives. To how many travelers did he become a fellow traveler through his prayer, and a pilot to those sailing in rough seas, especially in a violent storm? Whenever he saw the swell of the sea rising wildly and its roar overpowering the ears, he would urge the brothers to fervent prayer for those at sea and to sing that prophetic verse: “Were you angry with the rivers, Lord? Was your wrath against the rivers, or your fury against the sea?” And once the sea had calmed, one could see people coming and reporting their rescue through the holy man. “In our time of need,” they said, “you were seen sailing with us and steering the ship, standing at the stern and handling the rudder most skillfully.” And so they all glorified
Such were the distinctions of our honored Father Stephen on the island. In the second year of his residence and exile, the truly pious, child-loving woman of Abraham's line,

a new Sarah, not much inferior to the first, the [?] … [?] … the crafty dragon ordered the saint to sail back from Proconnesus, saying that he [?] ceases teaching the people to worship idols. When he had returned from Proconnesus, he ordered him in [?]…

…[not] answering, but bowing his head to the ground, the tyrant glared at him in anger, his eyes shot with blood, waved his hand in the air, and hissing loudly like a dragon said: “Will you not answer me, you most abominable head?” The saint said to him: “Emperor, if you wish to condemn me, punish me; but if you wish to question me, let gentleness keep your anger in measure. For this is how the laws command judges to judge.” The emperor said: “Tell me, what definitions and commandments of the Fathers have we refused to submit to, that you consider us to bear the mark of heretical opinion?” The saint said: “The pictorial representation that from of old has been received and venerated everywhere by all the Fathers, which you have lawlessly removed from the churches, digging it out of them.” The emperor said: “Do not call them representations, unholy head, but idol-pictures. What justice is there in idols alongside holy things? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?” The saint said to him: “Emperor, Christians never ordained the worship of matter in icons. Rather, we venerate the name of what we see, being led up in mind to the originals as their source. Through this sight our ruling faculty, unfolded by doctrine and by the aim of piety, aspires to the lofty, soaring tabernacles of heaven, so as to be able to contemplate the greatness of such things. For assent to what one seeks is like a nest for the soul: it gives rest within itself to the mind's restless curiosity, as to a long, wandering flight.” The emperor said: “Is it right, then, to depict in sensible form and venerate through matter things that men have proclaimed to be infinite and hard to behold, and not even subtle to the mind [?], when none of such things lies within our knowledge, except only their infinity, as Gregory the Theologian says?” Then the saint said: “And what man in his right mind who venerates the things in the church, whether stone or gold or silver, worships created things, since they have been made holy by the invocation? But you made no distinction between holy and profane, and did not shudder to call the icon of Christ, in your drunken insolence, an idol like Apollo, and likewise that of the Theotokos an idol like Artemis, and to trample on them and burn them.” The emperor said: “You blind-minded wretch, more worthless than the worthless! By trampling icons, have we trampled Christ? Far from it!” Then Stephen the wonderworker, who always carried Christ within himself and was wholly taught by him, drew his hand back to his breast, slipped it inside his holy cowl, brought out a coin bearing the image and name of the accursed one, and showed it to him, as Christ once did to the synagogue of the Jews, saying: “Whose image and inscription is this, emperor?” The tyrant, taken aback, said: “The reigning emperors'.” The saint said:

“Then if I throw this on the ground and deliberately trample it, will I be punished?” Those standing by said: “Certainly, because it bears the image and name of the invincible emperors.” The saint groaned deeply and said: “If that is what you say, what pitiable punishment will he suffer who has trampled and burned the name of Christ and of his Mother in an icon? Will he not surely be handed over to the unending, eternal fire and to the worm that never sleeps?” And he threw down the coin and trampled it. Those attending the emperor rushed at the saint like wild beasts and wanted to hurl him down the slope from the terrace. But the emperor, with a certain cunning (for he could disguise himself like a snake), shooed them away from doing this. At once he sent the saint, bound by the neck with his hands tied behind him, to the public prison of Byzantium, at the place called the sacred Praetorium, so that he might be tried according to law for having lawlessly trampled the emperor's image. What madness! Those who had openly transgressed the law of God and trampled his image make the law their champion over an image [?]. Who would not laugh at their folly? When our all-blessed Father Stephen was taken to the Praetorium, as soon as he entered the doorway his heart grew hot within him, to speak in the prophet's words, and the fire of his meditation was kindled, and he spoke with his tongue, foretelling the end of the days of his life: “This is where my life will come to rest, and here I will dwell until the last breath of my life, for I have chosen this place for the sake of the icon that bears Christ's name.” He found confined there a choice company of those who wore the holy monastic habit, about three hundred and forty-two in number, from various lands. Some had their noses cut off, others their eyes put out, others had their hands cut off for refusing to sign against the holy icons, and others had no ears. Some showed the marks of indescribable beatings. Others showed that they had no hair, having been shaved by the impious icon-burners, and most of them had their venerable beards smeared with pitch and [?]. When the saint saw these harsh and manifold punishments of the initiates of true piety, he gave thanks to God, who had granted them endurance. But he was vexed and distressed that he himself had not yet experienced any torture or lost a limb for this cause. All these Fathers received him as their chief shepherd and guide to salvation; they were taught by him and confided their thoughts to him. From then on the Praetorium became a monastery, with the whole monastic rule being observed. Those who had been entrusted with guarding the prison, and all

[?] …who had long been hearing of the holy man's reputation saw him truly keeping the divine image in him unspoiled, a true angel on earth, and they were astonished. One of the jailers even said to his own wife, as if in confidence, just like Manoah of old: "We are lost, wife, because of this tyrant's madness. For I have seen as it were God: Stephen, the son of Auxentius, who has just been shut up in the prison." That honorable woman, the new [?] and Shunammite, a true Phoebe, so to speak, and Tryphaena, plied her husband with question after question and so stole from him, by listening, the whole way of life of the blessed man. Then, secretly from her husband, she slipped into the prison, threw herself at the holy man's feet, asked for his prayer, and begged that from then on she might minister to the saint's needs. "Do not pass me by, Father," she said, "utterly wretched as I am, for I wish to bring you what you need for your comfort. Do not loathe me, sinner though I am. For in this way I too hope to receive a reward from God. So do not thrust me away, unworthy as I am." The honored Father said a prayer over her but would not agree to take anything at all. The woman said to him: "Venerable Father, why do you refuse my [?] toward you? Even if my unworthiness drives me away, your piety still knows how to show compassion. The widow of Zarephath once gave Elijah her flour; the Shunammite gave Elisha a room in hospitality; the widow praised in the Gospels put the two coins of her poverty into the treasury; and the Samaritan woman gave him, I mean Christ, the refreshing water of the very deep well. In the same way I too, persevering in something similar in the hope of faith, pray that I may not be turned away from you humbled and put to shame." The saint said to her: "Go away, woman, go away, for I cannot accept anything from you. It is not your nature or your unworthiness that I shun. God forbid! I am in every way pitiable and unworthy myself. But I am forbidden by the one who commands us not to have communion with heretics. And I know of no time when I have had communion with heretics who accuse Christians and burn icons, or received anything from their hands." When that Christ-loving woman, who loved the saints and was truly a guardian of the oppressed, heard this from the saint, she threw herself to the ground and cried out: "God forbid, holy Father Stephen, that I should ever insult an icon of Christ, or of his Mother, or of the saints! For I know what penalty those who have dared to do this will pay. Our father among the saints, Germanus, ranked those who destroy the holy icons

with those who cried out, 'Away with him, away with him, crucify the Son of God!' So, honored Father, I ask only this: that the matter be kept hidden from my husband and his fellow guards. And I will prove it to your holiness by deed." With these words she went back into her own house, opened her chest with its key, and brought out three hidden icons: one of the all-holy Theotokos holding in her arms her Son and God, and two of the chief apostles, Peter and Paul. She venerated them faithfully [?] and gave them to him, saying: "Holy one, let these stand before your face when you pray, so that you may also remember me, the sinner." The holy Father accepted her request, since it was made in this God-loving way. From then on, every Saturday and Sunday she brought him a little bread, about six ounces, and three small flasks of water. This was the blessed man's food and drink for the eleven months he spent in the praetorium.

One day, as the holy man was sitting with the Fathers who were his fellow prisoners, the conversation turned to the tortures of the persecution that the tyrant's governors had inflicted in the provinces. Antony from the island of Crete was brought forward to tell of a sacrifice offered to God. He said: "Honored Fathers, how can I set before your eyes without tears the feats of the fearless Paul? This noble man was arrested by Theophanes, the chief governor of the island, surnamed Lardotyros, and brought for examination in the so-called praetorium of Heraklion. On the ground lay the image of Christ as he was crucified for us, and beside it the instrument of torture that the Greeks call the katapeltes. The governor said: 'Paul, one of two things lies before you: either trample on the icon and live, or be [?] by torture.' But Paul cried out in a loud voice: 'God forbid, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, that I should trample on your divine icon, made in the likeness of your flesh, which is a dwelling place of your fearful name!' And bowing to the ground, he gave the holy icon its due veneration. The governor was enraged and ordered him stripped and then stretched out on the katapeltes. The attendants bound the saint tightly to the two boards from neck to ankles, nailed his limbs with irons, and hung him head down. Then they kindled a huge fire all around him. So this man, more lawless even than the lawless emperor, made the saint a whole burnt offering by fire."

While Antony was still speaking and all the Fathers were in tears, Theosteriktos came forward. He was an aged priest of the holy monastery of Pelekete, whose nose had been cut off and whose beard had been [?] with pi[tch?] [?]

[?] and naphtha, smeared on and set alight by the godless icon-burners. Coming forward into the midst, he said: "Is it not impossible, honored Stephen, to bear without weeping, or even to bring before one's eyes, the darkness and savagery of those days under the governor of the land of Asia, whom they call Lachanodrakon?" The honored Stephen said to him: "Speak, Father. For the Lord's sake speak, and do not hide anything. For you make us more eager, if God wills that we too should enter the contest." And Theosteriktos went on: "Holy Lent had passed and holy Easter was near. Late on Holy Thursday, the day on which Christ our God was handed over to the Jews, while the divine liturgy was being celebrated, this chief governor, who is named after a dragon, burst in at the emperor's command with a crowd of soldiers. At once they profaned the mysteries. They seized the leading monks, thirty-eight in number, and locked their hands and necks in wooden stocks. As for the rest, some he flogged without mercy and others he burned. He smeared the beards of others with pitch, set them on fire, and sent them away with their noses cut off. I myself am one of them. And not satisfied with this, that impious man burned down the whole monastery, from the stable to the churches, until he had reduced it to dust and razed it to the ground. Then he took those thirty-eight Fathers with him and shut them up in the vault of an old bath near Ephesus. He blocked the entrance, dug away the adjoining part of the hill, and buried them. And so, by unbearable violence, they were perfected in [?]"

When these grievous things, and many other painful ones, had been told, no one could hold back their tears. Then they asked holy Stephen to speak a word of encouragement now, as he used to do on the mountain. The all-blessed man sighed from the anguish of his soul and said: "Let us give thanks, Fathers and brothers, let us give thanks for all these things that have happened. For it is thankful endurance to the end that wins the crown. Even if fire, and sword, and sea, and finally death lie before us at the hands of the impious, let us endure. Let us imitate the holy Fathers of our own time who ended their lives as martyrs. I mean the holy Peter, the recluse at Blachernae. He was beaten with countless ox-hide whips before the emperor's face for the image of Christ, and he openly proclaimed the emperor a Datian and an apostate. Then he raised his eyes to God, said, 'I thank you, Lord,' and so breathed his last under the blows. And after him there was John, the godly abbot of the delightful monastery of Monagria. The tyrant emperor seized him tyrannically because he would not trample on the very image of Christ and of his Mother, shut him up in a sack, tied him to a great stone, and drowned him in the depths of the sea. What could be more pitiable than such a death? Yet it wins a more glorious [Variant readings: "of soul"; "openly proclaimed before all"]

crown. But let us stop here. For who could ever tell of all the devices and terrible tortures used in every province by the tyrant's governors, who were even more terrible than he, and enemies of the truth? Many are the trophies of their impiety, but let us spit on them and emulate the death of the Master. For the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us, as Paul, the chosen vessel, says."

But now the moment calls me, faithful and Orthodox audience, to bring to light the death of our venerable father Stephen for the sake of true religion. As I have pleaded many times already, my unworthiness holds me back, along with my complete ignorance of the art of speaking. But since the saint is sympathetic and kind toward my lowliness, and you are like him in your readiness to listen, I will not stop telling the story as well as I can, falsifying nothing of the truth.

God, who reveals his mysteries to his servants the prophets and makes known things before they happen, did not hide from our venerable father Stephen the time of his departure from this world. For, as was said above, the venerable Stephen had also received the gift of foresight. Forty days before his martyrdom, this honored and holy man called for that all-blessed and hospitable woman, the new [?], who ministered to the saints in prison, and said to her: "May the Lord give you the reward for your service to me, woman. I wish and intend to complete this forty-day prayer in stillness and abstinence, so stop bringing me the bread and the water." That honorable woman answered: "Why do you train yourself so harshly, Father? Has not the whole span of your life been one long fast, prayer, and hardship?" And the saint said: "I have learned that the short span of my life will [?] within a few days." Having moved the hospitable woman to compunction and won her over to his wish, he sent her away in peace. And so, all the days of that forty-day period, he never stopped talking with the Fathers who were his fellow prisoners and teaching them not to lose heart in their afflictions. He held all-night hymnody, so that some of the pious people of the city disguised themselves in [?] clothing and slipped into the prison to be blessed and taught by him. When these days had passed and the thirty-eighth day had arrived, early in the morning, after the dawn doxology and the dismissal of the First Hour, he again called for that much-blessed visitor, and in the Fathers' hearing he said: "Come, honored and blessed woman. Behold, the [?]

[?] …the unfailing [?], repaying you the fruits of your labors a hundredfold, as it is written in the Gospel. For you are truly a disciple of the one who said, 'Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me,' and, 'Whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man will receive a righteous man's reward.' So may the Lord give you a hundredfold, and number you with those faithful Marys and wise women, the Marys of Clopas and of Joses, of Joseph and of Joachim, and with Martha." After he had prayed these things and more over her, he took the divine icon of the Savior, made in the likeness of his flesh, and those of his disciples Peter and Paul, and gave them to her, saying: "Let these be a fortress for you in life and a pledge of the Orthodox faith." Then, with a great groan, he declared: "Tomorrow I depart from here and go to another world and another judge." She wept bitterly. She took back from the saint the holy icons she had brought earlier and wrapped them in a cloth for fear of the godless icon-burners. Then she left the prison once more and went home [?].

The Father then gathered the whole band of his fellow prisoners and had them perform an all-night service of hymns. Meanwhile the Dragon, emperor in name and tyrant in nature, who performed every pagan libation in the most abominable way, was at that time celebrating the Brumalia, that is, a demonic festival [?], in which he hailed Dionysus and Brumus as the creators of seed and wine. On that day, from early morning, he sat in the porticoes of the Scholae with his like-minded lyre-singers, rehearsing an obscure and God-hating piece for the libation that was under way. In it they had reached the letter that was fifth in order, which belonged to the name of his third, adulterous wife, Eudocia. Then some Christ-haters reported to him that Stephen son of Auxentius, the leader of the "Unmentionables," had turned the praetorium into a monastery and was holding all-night hymnody [?], and that everyone in the city was running to him to be taught idolatry. When the tyrant heard this, he boiled over with rage. He summoned a sword-bearing man who held the rank of Proximus and gave him an order: he was to take the holy man outside the city to the place where the venerable church of the holy and gloriously victorious martyr Maura had stood. That hater of the saints had razed it to the ground and turned it into a place of slaughter, and named the place Maura. There he also made his pacts with the demons. The child of Souphlamios, given as a sacrifice, bears witness to this, but there is no time to tell that story. Then he immediately ordered interrogations and searches to be made in the city. Anyone who had a relative or [?] connected with the monastic order, or even a black-dyed garment, [?] after seeing the gloating of enemies, they handed over whomever they wished. [References: Matt. [?]; [?]]

Slaves denounced their masters. There was lamentation and wailing in Byzantium greater than in the old days of the godless Julian and Valens. That Proximus took the holy man out of the praetorium, put a wooden yoke around his neck and hands, and hurried him off to the appointed place. Meanwhile the tyrant came out of the palace and was going to the public square on the avenue, the place called the Milion. In this public place the six holy ecumenical councils had been depicted since ancient times by those who had reigned piously long ago. They were displayed openly, proclaiming the Orthodox faith to country folk, strangers, and citizens alike. In those days the new Babylonian tyrant smeared them over and erased them. In their place he had painted a satanic horse race and the demon-loving charioteer he called "Ouranikos," because he was dear to him, though the man was unworthy of heaven and earth. So he honored the charioteer above the holy Fathers. Who would not shudder and be astonished at this outrage, and laugh [?] at it, or rather weep over it? O my Savior, how boundless your forbearance and long-suffering were then! He sat down there in the place of the Milion, and while everyone acclaimed and glorified him, he said: "My soul has no comfort because of these pestilent Unmentionables." One of his initiates answered, crying out: "And where, Master, has any trace or memory of them appeared in your city, or in any other land? All of them have been wiped out completely. Why, today I met Stephen son of Auxentius, the enemy of the truth, and saw him being led away to pay by the sword the penalty his crimes deserve." That shape-shifting Dragon said to him: "And what could be sweeter to Stephen than to receive capital punishment? I am convinced he has longed for it ever since he was imprisoned. He must not suffer such a death, but one more painful and harder to devise. Besides, the empress will be very upset with us if we end the day of her Brumalia feast with bloodshed." At once this new Herod, slave to a woman, ordered the holy man to be brought back and shut up in the prison again. And the Father, back in the praetorium with his fellow prisoners, sang once more in the words of David: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High," and the rest of the psalm.

That evening the tyrant performed his God-hating rite with shouting and lyres, and then lay down to drink. He summoned two brothers, born of the same father and mother, who held high rank. They were handsome in appearance and in soul, and greatly admired; later, out of jealous envy, he had them murdered.

He said to them: "Go [?] and say this to Stephen son of Auxentius: 'See how much I care for you, the emperor tells you. I snatched you from the very jaws of death and granted you life, so that you might bring yourself, at least at the very end, to do what pleases me most.' But I know his unbending and hard-hearted mind, and he will certainly turn to insulting us. Still, if you can win him over by persuasion, well and good. If not, beat him on the mouth and on the back so hard that, wretch that he is, he will die the moment you leave." That honorable pair of brothers went to the praetorium, came to the saint, and told him the emperor's words. They did the holy man no harm whatsoever; instead they strengthened him in the Orthodox faith. They kissed his feet, received his prayer, and went back to the one who had sent them. They said to him: "Emperor, since he still clung to his former views and uttered anathemas, we beat him so badly that he lies speechless. We say he will not live until tomorrow." The braggart was overjoyed and laughed loudly, and that slave of his belly went on with the gluttony of his Herodian drinking party.

Around dawn the holy man rose. He spent the time until morning with the band of Fathers, and then he said: "Farewell, Fathers and [brothers?], farewell. Pray for me, that no evil angel may be found to meet my spirit because of the great number of my debts." They all wept bitterly. He ordered his epomis, his analabos, and his belt to be taken off him. When he wanted to take off his cowl as well, the Fathers stopped him, saying: "No, holy Father. It is right that you be perfected wearing the holy habit." But the holy man said: "Fathers and brothers, a wrestler fights naked. And I do not think it right that this holy habit should be dishonored and trampled on by a people barking like dogs." With these words he persuaded the Fathers. Then, wearing only his leather tunic, he sat with them and talked about salvation.

That braggart of an emperor, however, learned through the night-raven demon what had happened with the holy man in the prison and how those pious brothers had deceived him. About the second hour of the day he got up from sleep, roared like a lion, and rushed out into the imperial vestibules, shouting violently: "Help! Is there no one to help me? What have I to do with these Unmentionables?" His invited guests, slaves to their bellies, were hurrying to the feast. He met them and said: "Where are you going, and whom are you looking for?" They said to him: "To you, most [?]" [Variant readings: "at the very end"; "wretch that he is" (alternative spelling); "they reported to him the emperor's madness, [harming the saint] in nothing," etc.]

[?] … our master, to rejoice with you, the great emperor, on the feast day of the Augusta now being celebrated.” But he answered back: “I am not emperor. Your emperor is someone else: you roll at his feet, kiss his footprints and beg for his prayers. No one is of one mind with me to kill him, so that my life may have some rest.” They were at a loss and asked, “Who on earth could be emperor above you, master? Do not be angry with us.” He said, “Stephen the son of Auxentius, the ringleader of the unmentionables.” As soon as the name was spoken, you could see that gang stirred up into a commotion like a clap of thunder. They ran to the praetorium, and when they got there they burst into the prison like wild beasts and shouted murderously at the jailers: “Give us Stephen the son of Auxentius, here!” That man, great in holiness, came out to them calmly and said, like a sheep to those who want to slaughter it, “I am the one you are looking for.” At once they threw him to the ground like wild beasts, tied ropes to the irons that locked his feet, and dragged him into the public street, kicking his head and his whole body, stoning him and beating him with clubs. As he was dragged out through the first gate of the praetorium, he reached the porch of the venerable chapel of the holy great martyr Theodore that stands there. He pressed his hands against the ground, lifted his head a little, raised his eyes to heaven, and venerated the martyr in a last farewell. One of the godless saw the saint do this. Wholly clothed in Satan, he gnashed his teeth and said, “Look, the unmentionable wants to die like a martyr!” He ran to the fire-fighting water pumps standing in that place, which they call siphons, and took from one of them a large wooden beam, which they call an antion. He swung it back in a rage, caught up with the saint as the crowd dragged him along, struck him on the skull as one would a dog, and killed the saint on the spot. This executioner went by the name of Philomates. He was at once thrown down, and was seen possessed by a demon and gnashing his teeth [?], and until his death he was tormented by the demon in this way. [Variant readings: “idolaters”; “where … were”; “Philomatius”; “reins.”]

[?] … burst open. You could see all the organs of the belly, together with the intestines, dragged horribly along the ground in full view. Truly, nothing more terrible than such a death was ever seen even among the pagans. For even after he had breathed his last, they kept beating the dead body with stones and clubs. Not only men but women and children too left their occupations at the tyrant’s order and ran with stones. And if anyone met this whole burnt offering sacrificed to God and did not strike it with stones, he was called to account as the saint’s friend and an enemy of the emperors. When those dragging him reached the place called the Ox, a tavern keeper who was frying fish in a pan saw the saint being dragged along the street. Thinking he was still alive, he grabbed a burning brand from the fire and struck the saint’s head [?]. He broke off the back part of the skull, which is called the hemicranium, and the fine, soft matter of the brain spilled onto the ground. A pious man named Theodore was secretly following behind. He pretended to slip, stooped to the ground, picked up that holy relic, [?] with his knife, and hid it inside his clothes. Then he hurried after the procession, wanting to see where they would throw the saint as food for dogs. That wicked crowd came, dragging him, to the monastery of Monokionion, where the saint’s sister was, to bring her out so that she might stone her brother and martyr with her own hands. But that honorable woman, truly the saint’s sister both by nature and by disposition, knew of the attack in advance. She shut herself in a dark tomb and so escaped their attempt. When the impious failed to find her, they dragged the saint from there again and flung him into the pit for pagans and condemned criminals, where the church of the holy martyr Pelagius used to be. The saint-hating tyrant had found it collapsed and had made it a burial place for the condemned, and he named it Ta Pelagiou. So the prophetic word was plainly fulfilled: “And the righteous one was counted among the lawless.” From there the brigands returned to the emperor as if they had fought bravely in some war, and he received them most gladly. And so the tyrant sat down with them at a table loaded with meats, heard about the saint’s many-sided death, and laughed loudly, to his own disgrace. The holy one of God, the holy martyr Stephen, was perfected in the fifty-third year of his age, in the month of November, on the twenty-eighth, on the day when the [?] … [Variant readings: “burst”; “collapsing.”]

… letter E is paraded by the demon-loving celebrants of the Brumalia. Therefore, beloved, it is not right to consign to silence the wonderful things that happened after the holy man’s death too, which the God of all did for the praise and glory of his servant. For he himself cries out in Scripture: “Those who glorify me I will glorify, and those who despise me shall be dishonored.” While the saint was being dragged to that bitter and merciless death, the air had been mild and the weather fair since dawn, and the sun’s rays shone until the third hour. Then suddenly a fiery cloud formed over the eastern part of Constantinople, toward the summit of the mountain from which the saint had come. As it reached the outskirts of the city, it darkened the whole sky. You could see day and yet not day, darkness and yet not night. A violent storm blew up, and so great a mass of hail poured down on the city, and on the city alone, that many were in danger as it came crashing down, and it did no small damage to the green fields within the city. The pious people who remained wept in secret and sought to appease God, that respite might be granted from the unbearable danger [?] with most faithful women. And God, who hears the prayer of those who fear him, did this, to the greater exposure and reproach of the impious emperor, unworthy of the purple. Theodore, the God-loving man mentioned above, who had taken the broken-off relic of the skull and hidden it in his bosom, went back after the saint had been thrown away and came to the most holy monastery of our holy father Dios. He took the superior of the monastery aside to a secret place, entrusted the relic to him, and told him what had happened to the saint that day. The abbot lamented greatly and groaned deeply. He took the God-loving Theodore up into the monastery’s right-hand chapel, dedicated to the holy protomartyr Stephen. He brought out a small casket and shut the saint’s holy relic inside it. A certain small boy named Stephanites, of this same monastery, was also present. Both men venerated it and placed it within the altar and the sacred enclosure, and kept the memory of it to themselves alone. After a short time, certain haters of Christ denounced the God-loving man Theodore to the emperor as a venerator of icons. The dragon of the deep ordered the man to be led into exile with his wife and children to the island of Sicily, and this was done at once. Many years passed, and the God-loving man was forgotten in exile. I shall now tell how God, who judges justly, restored him to his own people through the holy martyr Stephen.

When the boy Stephanites mentioned before reached the proper age, he asked his abbot to ordain him deacon. The abbot kept putting it off, because the boy was still young, and also because he knew his character, having brought him up with his own hands from an early age. When Stephanites failed to get what he asked, he threatened the abbot, stole the casket that held the saint’s relic, and rushed into the palace. He reported the whole affair to the tyrant: “My abbot,” he said, “venerates the bones of the enemies you have killed and calls them saints, and he denounces you as a tyrant and a new Julian, together with Theodore, who was exiled [?] of Dalmatou.” The tyrant boiled over with rage. At once he ordered the abbot to be [?] in handcuffs in prison and Theodore to be brought back quickly from Sicily to pay the penalty for his daring. He ordered the informer to guard the casket carefully until both men could be cross-examined in person. When the man had returned and reached the Queen City, the emperor called in the traitor alone, instructed him about the case against the righteous men, and dismissed him, telling him to bring the casket to the confrontation. The next day, when the three stood before the tyrant, the traitor accused both the abbot and the God-loving Theodore before everyone. If they were not convinced, he said, he would show the hour and the day, and the bloodied knife together with the relic. Those God-loving men denied it, maintaining that none of what was said was true. The emperor shouted at the traitor to bring out the casket as proof, the casket he had hidden [?], so as to show it as evidence. Then there was an astonishing sight: in an instant it vanished, and it has not been found to this day. At this the many-faced tyrant was put to shame all the more. Fearing that such a miracle might become known to the people of Byzantium (for many called him a saint and knew him as one), he had that enemy and traitor beaten unbearably and then exiled to a foreign land. And even against his will he restored the honorable men to their homes. They glorified God for everything, who had worked wonders through his saint so that they were kept safe. And what of that deceitful slave girl, about whom we wrote above? Taught by the impious, she slandered and accused her mistress and the saint, having received promises from them that she would be freed and married to one of the palace officials. It is not right to pass over in silence the end of life she met, in a most hateful and evil death. After her mistress had died a victor’s death from that unbearable beating, and the saint had been perfected through martyrdom, she had received none of what had been promised her. [Variant readings: “Deleiopou balai”; “of certain persons.”]

So she rose up against Callistus, mentioned earlier, and the tax collector Aulikalamos, saying, “Unless you fulfil what was promised me, I will proclaim in the middle of the city your villainies and your slanders against the saint.” They were at a loss, and after taking counsel they married her to a certain notary of the tax collector of Nicomedia, the same man. When the time came for her to give birth, this young viper bore two children [?]. Some time later she was alone, apart from her husband, and slept by herself between her children. Around midnight the babies fell into a frenzy, rose up, seized both her breasts, and devoured them, these viper’s brood. And so when day came, they found the mother and the babies dead, the babies still holding the bloodied flesh of the breasts in their teeth. This was the pitiable punishment that the deceitful slave girl, the accuser of the holy man, suffered. She ended her life wretchedly and was sent off to unending punishment. And in this God is not unjust, who swiftly destroys deceitful lips and the boastful tongue, to use David’s words, but glorifies those who glorify him even after death. These are the true accounts in this least of works of mine, gathered from the holy man’s relatives, acquaintances, kinsmen, housemates, neighbors and disciples, and also from the tyrant’s accomplices who are still living in this life. But you, honored Father, most holy Epiphanius, successor to the same hill, the same cave and the same way of life, who commanded and urged my humble self to this undertaking, overlooking my lack of learning and my sluggishness: may you receive what I offer, a few things out of many, gathered without any hesitation, with the eloquence of your prayers, acceptable to God, as my helper in this work. And what shall I say to you, holy Father and martyr, prize-winner, Stephen, rightly named the crown of prize-winners? Your martyrdom surpasses what is human, and those whose deeds are exceptional deserve praise beyond what is human. Therefore, having partly opened up the gloom of my perplexity through your intercessions, I honor you by making your deeds shine, and bringing you what is yours, like flowers from meadows, I sing the praises of your God-crowned joy. And as I bring you these gifts, I ask that my soul, worn down by many sins, be set free from the terrors that hold it fast. O martyr of God, who alone imitated the Master Christ by suffering for his image and shedding your blood; O new guardian and [?] champion of our race; O destroyer of demons, overthrower of the error of idols and venerator of holy icons; O physician of the sick and banisher of every kind of disease; O … [Variant readings: “table companions”; “therefore.”]

… defender of the oppressed and calm harbor for the storm-tossed; O provider for the poor and unfailing comfort of strangers; O guide of those who have gone astray and support of those who already believe rightly; O luminary of the whole world, enlightening souls darkened by heresy; O companion of angels and fellow dancer of archangels; O servant of the Holy Trinity and priest of human souls; O prayer offered acceptably to God for those who receive and glorify your martyrdom in true faith; O one who drives away, by God’s power, those who still persist in the heresy of the accusers of Christians, who like a deaf asp stop their ears, unwilling to hear or believe your athletic contests; and to put it briefly, O righteous one, who surpass every good name and every nobler deed, ornament of ascetics, choicest of the holy, bond of monks, lamp of teachers, model for those under obedience, crowned together with the martyrs, Stephen: receive now this discourse from me, as a true servant of God the Word. Imitate Christ in this too, who praised the widow’s two mites above the costly offerings of others. Do not turn away the alabaster jar of my words, just as the Master Christ did not turn away the harlot’s, even if I do not bring the fragrant [?] of good works. Make your dwelling in my humble soul, as Christ did in the house of Zacchaeus. At the examination, levy toll on the devil who has levied toll on me. Draw me up from the deep, me who am drowned in passions. By your prayers give life to me, who am dead in transgressions. Bring to Christ me who have been estranged from him by my sins. Mix oil with wine as a compassionate physician, and heal the infirmities of my sinful body, so that I too, unworthy as I am, may come to enjoy healing of both soul and body through you. And as in this life, most blessed Stephen, I have become your namesake, so may I also share your lot there and stand at the right hand, with this whole orthodox assembly that faithfully acclaims you as a holy martyr among the martyrs, by the motherly intercessions of the all-holy Theotokos and of all the saints, together with your holy prayers, acceptable to God. And with this assembly I send up glory for all things to Christ, our God and King of all, who crowned you as your name foretold. To him belong honor and worship, with his Father who is without beginning and the life-giving and Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
